title: PHP releases emergency updates for critical remote code execution flaws
text:
October 21, 2026

|

Security intelligence

PHP releases emergency updates for critical remote code execution flaws

By Field Effect Security Intelligence Team

At a glance:

PHP released emergency updates on October 21, 2026 for CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619, vulnerabilities that can allow unauthenticated remote code execution in web-facing PHP deployments.

The vulnerabilities affect PHP itself rather than a specific application, exposing a broad range of websites and business applications that rely on PHP processing.

Early attack activity was reported shortly after disclosure. The scale of exploitation and number of compromised organizations remain unclear.

Threat summary
An emergency security release from PHP on October 21, 2026 addressed two vulnerabilities that can allow unauthenticated remote code execution.
The release followed the premature disclosure of vulnerability details, which prompted security researchers and defenders to prepare for rapid exploitation activity once patches became available. Early attack activity was reported shortly after disclosure, although the extent of successful exploitation remains unknown.
PHP is a server-side scripting language used to process web requests and generate dynamic content. It serves as the underlying runtime for technologies including:

WordPress

Drupal

Joomla

Magento

Laravel, and

Many internally developed business applications

Because the vulnerabilities reside in the PHP runtime itself, exposure is tied to the underlying PHP installation rather than any individual application.
CVE-2026-109618 affects PHP's handling of out-of-memory conditions during request processing. Under specific circumstances, PHP can terminate request processing while internal request structures remain partially initialized. Cleanup routines may subsequently operate on invalid data, creating a memory corruption condition.
The advisory describes multipart request scenarios capable of reaching the vulnerable code path. PHP states the vulnerability can allow unauthenticated remote code execution.
CVE-2026-109619 is a use-after-free vulnerability involving PHP's request state management. Request-owned state may remain accessible after the memory backing it has been released. A subsequent request handled by the same worker process can access stale state before initialization occurs, creating conditions that can allow unauthenticated remote code execution.
Exploitation happens remotely over HTTP and requires a crafted request to a PHP-handled web endpoint. The request needs no login, no user interaction, and no vulnerable application code, because both flaws trigger before application code runs. Internet exposure of any PHP-served site is the only access condition. PHP rates the risk highest for Apache with mod_php, where it has a demonstrated exploit triggered by a single request.
Both vulnerabilities are rated 9.2 on the Common Vulnerability Scoring System (CVSS) version 4.0.
The vulnerable component is the PHP interpreter, so updating a plugin, theme, or content management system leaves the flaw in place. PHP names PHP-FPM (FastCGI Process Manager), Apache with mod_php, php-cgi, FrankenPHP, and LiteSpeed as affected ways of running PHP.
Analysis
These vulnerabilities affect the runtime layer that many organizations depend on. A vulnerable PHP deployment may host multiple websites, APIs, customer portals, and business applications, allowing a single flaw to create exposure across several services simultaneously.
Successful exploitation provides code execution within the PHP process. The resulting impact depends on the resources available to that process, including application data, databases, stored credentials, cloud services, and internal systems accessible from the affected server. The scope of compromise is therefore highly dependent on how the server is deployed and what privileges have been granted to the application. 
Apache mod_php deployments warrant particular attention because […]

title: AOMEI Backupper supply chain attack
text:
October 21, 2026

|

Security intelligence

AOMEI Backupper supply chain attack

By Field Effect Security Intelligence Team

At a glance:

On October 15, Google disclosed a supply chain campaign targeting AOMEI Technology's update infrastructure between April and July 2026.

The activity was attributed to threat actor UNC7017, which distributed the CROSSROAD downloader and SHINYROAD backdoor through temporary modifications to AOMEI update services.

Organizations that used AOMEI Backupper and checked for updates during the brief compromise windows were at risk of receiving malware from trusted vendor infrastructure.

Threat summary
On October 15, 2026, Google Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG) disclosed a software supply chain campaign targeting the update infrastructure of AOMEI Technology. The affected infrastructure supported:

AOMEI Backupper, a Windows backup, disk cloning, and disaster recovery platform

AnyViewer, a remote desktop and remote support application

Both products rely on the same ABMarket update mechanism and associated background services, including Backupper.exe and ABNotify.exe, which periodically connect to AOMEI-operated servers over HTTPS to retrieve update notifications and promotional content.
Between April and July 2026, threat actor UNC7017 repeatedly modified two configuration files hosted on that infrastructure for periods lasting five to ten minutes. Systems that checked for updates during those windows received malicious instructions, while systems that connected before or after received legitimate content.
Researchers observed compromise windows on May 28, July 16, and July 20, 2026.
The modified configuration files redirected AOMEI clients to download a malicious ZIP archive from adversary-controlled infrastructure and automatically execute its contents through the application's notification workflow.
The archive contained a downloader tracked as CROSSROAD, which performs environment checks, retrieves additional payloads, creates a scheduled task for persistence, and removes itself from disk. The scheduled task launches SHINYROAD, a modular backdoor that provides remote access while operating through a legitimate signed Radmin component.
Researchers also observed deployment of the Adaptix command-and-control framework during later stages of the campaign, disguised as Nitro PDF-related software.
On July 20, 2026, UNC7017 introduced a second technique by modifying the notification configuration file to display an invisible one-pixel popup that directed systems to a remote Web Distributed Authoring and Versioning (WebDAV) resource. This activity caused affected systems to transmit New Technology LAN Manager (NTLM) authentication hashes to infrastructure controlled by the threat actor, creating a credential collection path in addition to malware delivery.
GTIG identified affected organizations in information technology services, telecommunications, and higher education across Australia, Brazil, India, Pakistan, Portugal, Singapore, South Africa, Spain, Switzerland, Türkiye, and the United States.
The campaign targeted any system that queried the update infrastructure during an active tampering window, indicating the victim pool may extend beyond the organizations directly identified during the investigation.
Analysis
Organizations using AOMEI Backupper on backup servers, recovery systems, and administrator workstations would be the most exposed. These systems often hold privileged access and visibility into large parts of the environment, making them attractive targets for threat actors seeking access to sensitive data or additional systems within the network.
What makes this campaign notable is that UNC7017 did not need to compromise customer environments directly. By modifying configuration files on AOMEI's infrastructure, the actor was able to control where clients downloaded content from, what files were accepted as valid updates, and what content was executed. Affected systems carried out […]

Keep Calm, and Patch PHP2Shell
text:
Keep Calm and Patch PHP2Shell

October 21, 2026

Justin Timothy

With contributions by the GuidePoint Security GRIT team

BLOG

How to Respond to CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619

*Note: This is an actively developing situation and the information from this blog is accurate as of writing. Please refer to PHP’s official guidance for any newly released information and additional patching and mitigation recommendations.

The newly released ‘PHP2Shell’ vulnerabilities have become a hot topic hitting the desks, feeds and wires of every cybersecurity professional around the world. Starting October 20th, leaked details, disputed PoCs, conflicting exploitation reports and a patch that was scheduled but not yet released started circulating among security professionals online.

TL;DR – LPHP2Shell is a critical, highly exploitable set of two vulnerabilities that could potentially affect a massive percentage of internet facing websites. The patch is available and the time to patch is now.CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619, collectively nicknamed “PHP2Shell”, are critical severity vulnerabilities that require immediate attention. Patches are available for supported versions of PHP. PHP supplied Linux distributions and LTS vendors the patches in advance. Experts recommend isolating or decommissioning systems running versions older than 7.4.It’s important to patch internet-facing systems first, rebuild containers that contain PHP, restart all affected systems after patching and conduct retrospective threat hunts to ensure no threat actors slipped through before the patches were applied.

The instinct during these types of high-impact vulnerability disclosures is to either panic or wait for certainty. Panic can lead to uncoordinated patching and inconsistent workarounds. Waiting means the exploit code is circulating before you hit your change window.It wasn’t until PHP released their official post announcing the two CVEs and the mitigation options that the world was able to definitively understand the impact and start implementing patch management strategies.This is why a balanced approach works best: act on what’s confirmed, prepare for what’s coming and make deliberate decisions about the tradeoffs you’re accepting.

What We Know About PHP2Shell

All PHP installations serving web requests, including PHP-FPM, Apache with mod_php, php-cgi, FrankenPHP and LiteSpeed are affected by these vulnerabilities. PHP considers the risk highest for mod_php, where the demonstrated exploit achieves unauthenticated remote code execution before application code runs. Both CVEs have been rated CVSS 9.2 (Critical) under CVSS v4.0 by PHP.

CVE-2026-109618: RCE via OOM Corruption

PHP handles out-of-memory (OOM) conditions, unwinding straight out of the current execution context and aborting the request. In certain early-request contexts, request-scoped memory is reachable before it has been fully initialized.If any allocation fails in that window, the non-local exit skips the initialization and PHP’s error path does not account for the half-built state. The request shutdown routine then reads or branches on that memory. The failing allocation does not need to be related to the corrupted memory, so the trigger is generic: any OOM during the window is enough.Several OOM-induction strategies trigger it consistently, which makes exploitation reliable and leads to Remote Code Execution (RCE).

CVE-2026-109619: RCE Via Stale Global State

PHP workers are long-lived and reused across requests and they keep some global state (error, session, object and extension data) that points to memory belonging to a single request. That state should be cleared before the request’s memory is freed. A fatal error can stop an operation before it cleans up. Examples include running out of memory, hitting the execution time limit or a failed compile. A later warning during shutdown can also refill error state that was already cleared. The request’s memory is then freed while the […]

title: Protecting Against AiTM Attacks: Is Your Microsoft Environment at Risk?
text:
Protecting Against AiTM Attacks: Is Your Microsoft Environment at Risk?

October 21, 2026

Nick Schmitz

BLOG

The identity threat landscape has shifted considerably over the past few years. Attackers have steadily moved toward more sophisticated techniques and Adversary-in-the-Middle (AiTM) phishing is near the top of that list. Microsoft observed a 146% rise in AiTM attacks in 2024 and the trend has continued into 2026.

TL;DR – If your Microsoft 365 environment relies on traditional multifactor authentication (MFA) without phishing-resistant authentication and or layered Conditional Access policies, AiTM attacks can bypass your defenses and hijack active sessions in real time.Key Takeaways:AiTM phishing has been commoditized through Phishing-as-a-Service platforms. AI-generated lures have eliminated the visual cues that users once relied on to identify phishing attempts.Phishing-resistant authentication methods (FIDO2, passkeys, Windows Hello for Business, certificate-based authentication) are the only category of MFA that AiTM proxies cannot relay, making them the most critical control to prioritize.Deploying these controls in production environments with hybrid identity, legacy applications and third-party integrations requires deliberate sequencing and real-world risk assessment, not just baseline compliance.

A significant driver of AiTM growth is the Phishing-as-a-Service ecosystem. Platforms like Tycoon2FA have industrialized AiTM attacks. A threat actor with minimal technical skill can rent a fully functional proxy-based phishing kit, for as little as $120. The result is a category of attack that was once the domain of sophisticated threat actors and is now widely accessible.AI is accelerating this trend further. Phishing lures that used to be easy to spot, including awkward phrasing, odd formatting, generic greetings have all but vanished. Lures are increasingly generated by AI tools that produce polished, personalized and contextually convincing content at scale. Research has found that AI-generated phishing attacks are becoming increasingly common. For organizations running Microsoft 365, this is a practical problem worth understanding.

What is AiTM and How Does It Work?

AiTM attacks build on the foundation of traditional man-in-the-middle tactics. This type of attack operates across multiple communication layers, from the network and transport layers all the way up to the application layer, relaying traffic in real time. Once positioned, the attacker actively intercepts the exchange between the victim and the legitimate service.A user clicks a link in a phishing email and lands on an attacker-controlled reverse proxy. This proxy silently relays everything to the real login server. The user enters their credentials and completes their multi-factor authentication (MFA) challenge, if applicable. To the user, everything looks normal, even the sign-in page will display their organization’s branding.At the end of the authentication flow, once the server is satisfied, it issues a session cookie. The attacker’s proxy captures that token and injects it into their own browser. They now hold a valid, active session and can navigate everywhere the user can. Traditional MFA methods like Short Message Service (SMS) codes and number matching cannot prevent this.

What Native Microsoft 365 Controls Can Help Address AiTM Risk?

Microsoft 365 includes several controls that directly address AiTM risk. The most effective are phishing-resistant authentication methods, specifically Fast Identity Online 2 (FIDO2) security keys, passkeys, Windows Hello for Business and certificate-based authentication. These methods are cryptographically bound to the legitimate domain, meaning a proxy cannot relay them. They are the only authentication methods that can stop AiTM if setup properly.Beyond phishing-resistant authentication methods, Conditional Access is one of the most powerful tools available for reducing AiTM risk. Requiring compliant […]

title: AI Agents Are Redefining Credential Management
text: AI Agents Are Redefining Credential Management October 21, 2026 GuidePoint Security By Dave Lewis, Global Advisory CISO, 1Password BLOG It should come as no surprise at this point that AI agents are fundamentally changing the role of credential management  in respect to continuous identity and governance. The common thought process is that enterprises should inventory every agent, replace standing secrets with scoped and short-lived access and make every action attributable to an owner. But how do they get there? Being able to exercise control of your credentials is essential. But traditional methods of credential rotation were made to  deal with credentials for humans. Once you switch into governing credentials for AI agents, the playing field changes drastically. You never want to give a static credential to an agent that will live on in perpetuity. Once that credential is in the inference window, you’ve lost control of it. You want to be able to give agents just the right amount of access for the right amount of time, so they can do their one job and be done with it.Traditionally, credential management relied on managing the interaction between two forces: 1) the credential itself and 2) the identity using that credential. But over the past few decades, that equation has changed as passwords and credentials have evolved. Now we find ourselves in a real interesting quagmire where we’re dealing with human credentials, non-human identities (NHI), service accounts, secrets, machine account access keys and so on and so forth. How do we manage all of these and balance their various security risks and access needs?Most recently, AI agents have fundamentally changed and expanded how we define and manage the “identities” that interact with those credentials. The natural question on every leader’s mind this cybersecurity month should be: how can credential governance change to manage this new form of identity?Agents and NHIs challenge traditional identity modelsIn days of yore, identity and access management (IAM) could operate under certain assumptions about how a given identity will access systems. For instance, developers need access to the codebase, but not to company financial records, while finance teams have opposite needs. Beyond a few highly privileged users, it’s rare that anyone genuinely needs long-standing access to tools or systems that aren’t directly relevant to their role.AI tools and agents are a different matter entirely. For one task, an agent might need access to a database; for the next, it might need access to the company’s visual design assets. NHIs and AI agents require access to a much wider variety of systems and data than human users with static roles do, but providing them with long-lived access to those systems could be a recipe for disaster. Even when operating correctly, agents can interpret commands in extreme ways, such as in the PocketOS incident, in which an agent used a long-lived API token to delete an entire production database; teams need to ensure that they don’t have the access needed to make destructive decisions without oversight. 1Password’s research found that 47% of developers have had an AI agent follow instructions from a prompt injection attack and 74% of developers witnessed unintended consequences from using AI agents.Unfortunately, 1Password’s research also discovered that oversight into agent identities is severely limited; 40% of developers grant agents persistent access to systems or […]

title: Widespread PHP Flaw May Cause Many Site Outages Today
text:
Expect to see quite a few websites serving error pages today: Nearly 70 percent of websites need to update their core software to fix a pair of vulnerabilities that allow an attacker to seize full control over affected servers. Experts say there are working exploits for the flaws, and that these critical bugs are already being exploited in the wild.
Image: Shutterstock.com, Sashkin.
The flaws at issue are present in PHP, the programming language that powers sites running on a large number of web publishing systems, including Drupal, Magento, Joomla and WordPress. Earlier today, PHP released an emergency security update to fix two critical bugs that can allow an attacker to execute code of their choosing on a vulnerable server.
Reuters reports that government websites in Europe and elsewhere went offline today after the PHP vulnerabilities were disclosed. Cloudflare said it has already detected some exploitation of the flaw, and that at 3:02 am (UTC) it implemented web application firewall rules to protect websites from attack traffic seeking to exploit the bugs, which could cause a denial of service condition, remote code execution, and data exposure.
OpenAI, which was involved in the vulnerability research and outreach, said “given the severity of these flaws and PHP’s widespread use, we consider this one of the most impactful security issues in recent memory.”

Censys, a company that tracks the technology used by Internet hosts, said a recent scan identified approximately 2.58 million Internet facing hosts and 54.9 million web properties running PHP.
Security experts at Wiz said every PHP version released in the last decade is affected by at least one of these vulnerabilities [full disclosure: Wiz is an advertiser on this blog].
“These findings rank among the most severe vulnerabilities discovered in PHP, and arguably in software history,” reads a blog post published today by a team of researchers at Wiz, which was one of several organizations credited with discovering the vulnerabilities. “The underlying flaws had been present for decades, but demonstrating their exploitability required an exceptionally complex chain of steps, at the edge of what human researchers could practically achieve. Frontier AI models substantially reduced that barrier, turning a longstanding flaw into an exploit.”
The Wiz researchers say it is likely the PHP vulnerabilities will be mass-exploited to install web-based backdoors or “web shells,” which give attackers a web-based panel that allows them to remotely control infected sites. Wiz said that prior to the PHP bugs being publicly disclosed, the company worked with the PHP team, Calif and OpenAI to measure the size of the problem and coordinate patch verification and disclosure.
The PHP zero-day vulnerabilities are being tracked by their CVE numbers, CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619, and they affect all web servers running PHP 5.4 or later. The bugs are fixed in PHP 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36, and 8.2.35.
According to Wiz, PHP is so deeply embedded in many web applications that we are likely to see organizations struggling to patch these vulnerabilities for some time to come, comparing this PHP vulnerability pair with the Log4Shell weakness that emerged in 2021 — a widespread, severe-as-it-gets security flaw in Log4j, a popular Java logging framework.
“A vulnerability in core PHP reaches far beyond a single application,” the Wiz researchers wrote. “PHP runs across clouds, hosting providers, content-delivery networks and millions of independently managed servers. Reducing exposure before the technical details became public required coordinated work across that entire ecosystem.”
The SANS Internet Storm Center is keeping an eye on major software platforms that are shipping updates to deal with these PHP flaws. For example, Ubuntu just released updated PHP packages. title: PHP2Shell Exploitation: Two Critical PHP Flaws Explained
text:
PUBLISHED ON 21 OCT 2026

Insikt Group®

Summary

Two critical remote code execution vulnerabilities in the PHP engine, CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619 (nicknamed “PHP2Shell”), are reportedly being targeted in active exploitation attempts following the leak of technical details ahead of PHP’s October 21, 2026, security release. Because the flaws affect PHP itself rather than a specific application, websites running vulnerable PHP versions may be exposed, including those built on WordPress, Drupal, and Joomla.
This post covers PHP’s advisories, exploitation reports, public proof-of-concept exploits, exposure data, and patching guidance, along with details from the TTP Instance Insikt Group® published to customers. Attack Surface Intelligence signatures for CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619 are available to Recorded Future customers. Organizations running PHP should patch immediately.

The Latest UpdateInsikt Group has published a TTP Instance for PHP2Shell covering public proof-of-concept (PoC) exploits, observed exploit activity, and recommended mitigations. As of 7 PM UTC on October 21, 2026:
Patch status: PHP released fixed versions on October 21, 2026: PHP 8.2.35, 8.3.36, 8.4.27, and 8.5.12.
Exploitation status: While there are some reports of emerging exploitation attempts targeting PHP2Shell, the available reporting does not establish the full extent of successful exploitation or confirmed compromises (1, 2).
PoC status: Publicly available repositories claim to provide PHP2Shell proof-of-concept (PoC) exploits, although their effectiveness and relationship to the confirmed vulnerabilities vary. For example, security researcher J4ck3LSyN published two alleged PoCs but subsequently invalidated the cached-pointer UAF theory underlying their proposed exploitation sequences.
How It StartedOn October 20, 2026, the PHP security team announced an out-of-band security release for October 21 at 14:00 UTC to fix two critical vulnerabilities, both rated 9.2 under CVSS v4.0. PHP initially withheld technical details and affected versions pending coordinated disclosure, warning that the release could be accelerated if vulnerability details leaked or exploitation emerged.Ahead of the scheduled release, watchTowr reported reproducing CVE-2026-109618 and assessed that both vulnerabilities could enable remote code execution (RCE). Technical information subsequently leaked before coordinated disclosure, prompting heightened concern about potential exploitation. PHP shipped the fixes on October 21, alongside a PHP Foundation post about the release, which addressed the emergency release and improvements to PHP's security processes.The “PHP2Shell” name comes from Wiz Research, which found the flaws with Calif and OpenAI and reported them to PHP in August. Wiz’s write-up covers the discovery and root cause in depth.The VulnerabilitiesBoth CVEs are memory-safety vulnerabilities involving PHP's handling of request memory during initialization, error handling, and cleanup. According to Wiz, out-of-memory (OOM) failures and stale internal state can expose freed or partially initialized memory, potentially enabling memory disclosure, memory corruption, and remote code execution (RCE).
CVE-2026-109618: An OOM-related vulnerability involving partially initialized request memory. Wiz identified a use-after-free (UAF) in the session upload-progress unserializer and a related flaw that can disclose PHP worker memory. Wiz demonstrated unauthenticated RCE against WordPress, Drupal, and Joomla.
CVE-2026-109619: A stale-state vulnerability involving PHP globals that retain references to freed request memory. Wiz identified a UAF involving fatal-error backtraces and a separate OPcache type-confusion flaw. Wiz demonstrated unauthenticated RCE against Drupal and WordPress.

title: Critical RCE vulnerabilities in PHP (CVE-2026-109618, CVE-2026-109619)
text:
Threat Response

Vulnerability overviewDetection by Kaspersky solutions

Vulnerability overview
On October 20, 2026, the PHP security team published a preliminary notice regarding an upcoming emergency release that addresses two critical vulnerabilities (both rated 9.2 on the CVSS scale). The patches were released on Wednesday, October 21, 2026, at 14:00 UTC.
The release was expedited after information about the vulnerabilities was leaked to the public before the scheduled embargo was lifted. In a post on Hacker News, a user reported two RCE vulnerabilities in PHP, allegedly affecting all versions starting with PHP 5.4.0.
The vulnerabilities in question are CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619. Shortly after the post appeared, researchers confirmed the existence of the vulnerabilities. Along with the leak of details, an exploit unofficially named PHP2Shell appeared online. In the leaked demo video, the exploit is shown in action on web servers running WordPress, MediaWiki, phpBB, Magento, Joomla, Laravel, Symfony, Drupal, and WHMCS — platforms that power many modern websites. The authenticity of the demonstration and the exact behavior of the exploit had not been independently verified at the time of publication.
According to the researcher who published the PoC, the vulnerabilities are related to the handling of the multipart/form-data MIME type in conjunction with the session upload progress mechanism (session.upload_progress) in the PHP core and fall under the categories of use-after-free and memory corruption. This means that the flaws cannot be patched via application code, and the only possible fix is to update PHP on the server. The attack works without authentication: an attacker with network access to a PHP application can execute arbitrary code on behalf of the PHP process without needing to authenticate. Security advisories issued by PHP on October 21 confirm this information.
The vulnerabilities affect PHP versions 5, 6, 7, and 8. As of this publication, branches from 8.2 to 8.5 are supported. Older branches, including PHP 8.1, 8.0, 7.x, and 5.x, have reached the end of their lifecycle; however, due to the critical severity of the vulnerabilities, backported patches have also been released for versions 7.4, 8.0, and 8.1.
Sansec experts estimate that widespread exploitation could begin within 15 minutes of the update’s release. We strongly recommend that administrators responsible for publicly accessible PHP web servers take the following steps before the patch is available:

1 Conduct an inventory of all PHP-based systems in the infrastructure (including web servers, control panels, third-party software, etc.).
2 Disable upload-progress: set session.upload_progress.enabled = Off using the php_admin_flag in PHP-FPM pools.
3 Block multipart requests on nginx and Apache servers.
4 Consider temporarily isolating PHP applications that connect to the Internet until fixes are released.
5 Ensure readiness to install the patch immediately upon its release.
6 Plan to migrate servers running unsupported versions (8.1 and earlier) to the latest PHP branch.

Detection by Kaspersky solutions
Kaspersky solutions detect the described malicious activity at various stages of the attack. Possible detection scenarios are listed below.
When an attempt is made to exploit these RCE vulnerabilities, Kaspersky Endpoint Detection and Response promptly alerts the user to suspicious actions performed in the context of a web server, on both Linux and Windows machines. This activity is detected by the following rules:

creating_windows_shell_from_a_web_servers_process;
possible_web_shell_creating_via_exploit;
spawning_process_from_webserver_more_filters_linux;
webserver_interpreter_execution_linux;
executable_file_in_www_folder.

text:
BackgroundInitial infection vectorFull infection chainMalware setTechHub – the start of the chainCubridge – the framework orchestratorTouchHub installs a service for TouchShiftTouchShift, a prevalent loader employed across multiple infection chainsClientHubLPEClientComparison of plugins and modulesInfrastructureVictimsAttribution and links to other campaignsConclusionIndicators of compromiseFile hashesFile pathsC2 servers

Authors

Sojun Ryu

In January, we responded to the Lazarus Group’s novel attack campaign against South Korea, which followed last year’s Operation SyncHole. In this new operation, the group employed an updated malware chain that included both their old and new malware, which we disclosed in full, and used another mandatory South Korean security software program as a part of infection chain using a watering‑hole strategy. Notably, the group targeted victims more selectively, sending spear‑phishing emails with links to fabricated but relevant sites, such as portfolio and résumé pages tailored to each target. We dubbed this activity Operation FlashHole.
Operation FlashHole attack flow during initial compromise
Our examination reveals that the earliest evidence of this new operation dates back to July 2025. This suggests the group began preparing for the campaign shortly after ending Operation SyncHole, which lasted at least four months. We identified a minimum of three organizations impacted by the campaign in South Korea’s software, construction, and wired communication equipment manufacturing sectors. These sectors differ from those affected by Operation SyncHole, indicating that the group has expanded its target scope over time.
Background
After more than a year since the first observation of Operation SyncHole, we detected a suspicious execution chain originating from legitimate South Korean software. This chain mirrors the one from the previous operation; however, this time, the attacker abused CrossWeb EX instead of Cross EX, which was abused in Operation SyncHole. Both applications appear to be maintained by the same vendor, and both are related to financial security. CrossWeb EX is a financial security solution that is required to access widely used online banking and government websites. It encrypts communications between the user’s browser and the web server using public key infrastructure (PKI). This is not the first time Lazarus has abused this software. It was also used in 2021 to deploy the Racket downloader and again in 2022 and 2023. Although the exact method by which CrossWeb EX was abused remains unclear, we determined that the attack chain ultimately leads to the execution of the malware in memory.
We noted that the spawned process was running with a high integrity level. The parent process, INISAFECrossWebEXSvc.exe, originates from the installation bundle of INISAFE CrossWeb EX V3 version 3.4.1.2, released in 2023 after KrCERT’s public advisory.
As we already mentioned in our SyncHole blog post, this pattern closely mirrors the long‑standing strategy employed by the Lazarus Group to target South Korea. Since CrossWeb EX and similar software is mandatory for South Korean users and typically runs in the background to interact with the browser, it has been leveraged as a critical attack vector by the group. In 2025, a paper was presented at the USENIX Security Symposium that investigated vulnerabilities in South Korea’s mandatory security software and demonstrated how such software can unintentionally create a massive attack surface.
In July 2026, the South Korean government and several local security vendors also published a joint security advisory covering typical Lazarus attack techniques, including exploitation of financial security software. Pierluigi Paganini

A Russian satellite made a close approach to a commercial radar satellite linked to Ukraine, raising concerns about surveillance and security in space.

A Russian-made satellite called Kosmos 2612 got very close to ICEYE-X36 last week, a commercial Earth-observation satellite that may support countries like Ukraine. CNN reports it may have come within less than a mile. Orbital monitoring company LeoLabs says the behavior is consistent with rendezvous and proximity operations, meaning maneuvers designed to bring two spacecraft together.

“A rare move by a Russian-made satellite may have brought it within less than a mile of a commercial Earth-observation satellite that may be used to provide national security services to countries such as Ukraine.” states CNN.

“It’s not clear what, exactly, the Russian satellite, called Kosmos 2612 or Cosmos 2612, intended to accomplish with its close approach. But the behavior was consistent with rendezvous and proximity operations, or maneuvers carried out in orbit that are designed to bring two spacecraft together, said orbital monitoring services company LeoLabs, which tracks space junk and activity in Earth orbit, in a statement.”

It is unclear what Russia wanted to achieve. LeoLabs said “While the intent remains uncertain, the behavior warrants continued monitoring.” Astrophysicist Jonathan McDowell noted that this could be the first known case of one spacecraft approaching another without permission. This is different from docking, when two spacecraft intentionally connect, a common practice in space.

The events unfolded over several months. In May, four Russian-controlled satellites changed their orbits to align with ICEYE-X36, according to a June report by the Royal United Services Institute. title: Autonomous LLMjacking: ‘Skynet’ Agent Hijacks Exposed AI Models to Run Attacks
text: Key findingsAttackers have built an autonomous offensive agent that searches the internet for exposed large language model (LLM) endpoints and hijacks them to run its own attacks.The captured instructions defined a single agent equipped for internet-wide scanning, exploitation of several common web frameworks, database theft, credential and secret harvesting, and cryptocurrency mining.The agent was designed to run unattended for up to 100,000 steps, executing tools without waiting for human approval.The activity is a form of LLMjacking, where attackers steal access to someone else's AI model so that the victim pays for the computing power. To make a commercial model comply, the operators wrapped their requests in a jailbreak that told the model to ignore its safety controls and to treat credential theft as routine development work.OverviewAttackers have built an autonomous offensive agent that hunts the internet for exposed large language models (LLMs) and hijacks them to power a self-directed cybercrime operation. Once connected to an unprotected model, the agent is instructed to scan for new targets, exploit common web frameworks, steal databases and credentials, and quietly install cryptocurrency miners, for up to 100,000 steps and without asking a human for approval. The owner of the hijacked model pays for the computing power, while the servers the agent breaks into are stripped of data and put to work mining.The activity is a form of LLMjacking, in which attackers steal access to someone else's AI model. What sets this tool apart is that the stolen model does not simply answer questions; it plans and drives the attack. To make a commercial model cooperate, the operators wrapped their instructions in a jailbreak that told it to ignore its safety controls and to treat credential theft as routine development work. A directive the operators called “Skynet mode” described a loop that would scan for targets, infect them, deploy miners and reinfect hosts.Symantec captured the agent's full instruction set in the summer of 2026 through an AI honeypot, a system that impersonates an unprotected, internet-facing AI service in order to attract and study attacks against AI infrastructure. Because the operators sent the tool's entire working prompt to what they believed was a real model, the honeypot recorded an unusually complete view of how such an agent is built and what it is told to do. The request was not aimed at subverting the honeypot itself, but was sent in the expectation that a model on the other end would carry it out.What the attackers were looking forAn exposed LLM endpoint is a server that answers AI requests over the internet without authentication, or with authentication that a stolen key can pass. Because most AI tools now use the same OpenAI-compatible programming interface, a single scanner can find many kinds of target with one set of probes. These include self-hosted model servers left open by default, AI gateways and relays that sit in front of an organisation's paid model accounts, hastily deployed internal test systems, and Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers that connect a model to real tools.The prize is free inference. Running a model always costs someone money, either in processing time for a self-hosted model or in per-token fees for a commercial one. By routing its work through a stranger's endpoint or a stolen key, the operators shift that cost onto the victim. They also gain anonymity, avoid the account bans a provider would issue for abuse, and, where the endpoint fronts a commercial model, obtain a system whose safety controls they then attempt to strip. The honeypot's own telemetry, which recorded more than 127,000 external requests from tens of thousands of unique addresses over the period, was dominated by this kind of activity: reconnaissance of model endpoints, spraying of stolen API keys, and probing for exposed configuration files.Tooling and tradecraftThe request was built in layers. Log Analytics with LogTotal
text:
What Is Log Analytics?

Log analytics is the practice of collecting, parsing, normalizing, and querying machine-generated event records to answer an operational or security question. In a SOC, that question is usually narrow: did this account authenticate from an unexpected source, did this host spawn an unusual child process, which API calls preceded the data transfer.

The raw material is heterogeneous: Windows Security and Sysmon channels in .evtx files, Linux auth.log and journald output, firewall and proxy events in CEF, and cloud audit trails such as AWS CloudTrail or Microsoft Entra ID sign-in logs exported as JSON.

A working log analytics pipeline has four stages:

Collection. Export events from the source without losing fields or timestamps.

Normalization. Map src_ip, IpAddress, and sourceIPAddress to one common schema.

Detection. Run Sigma or vendor rules and tag every hit with MITRE ATT&CK techniques.

Correlation. Group related hits into a timeline or attack chain that an analyst can validate.

Why Log Analytics Matters for Detection and Response

Logs are often the only record that survives an intrusion. EDR telemetry rolls over, memory is lost on reboot, and packet capture is rarely running when you need it. Windows Event IDs 4624, 4672, and 4688, or CloudTrail calls such as ConsoleLogin and CreateAccessKey, are typically the primary evidence for scoping an incident.

Three pressures make log analytics a core SOC skill rather than a SIEM feature:

Volume. A single incident can produce millions of events, and grep only finds what you already know to look for.

Coverage gaps. Contractor laptops, OT segments, and SaaS tenants nobody connected are not in the SIEM, but their logs still need analysis.

Data handling. Logs carry usernames, hostnames, IPs, session cookies, and bearer tokens. Under GDPR much of that is personal data, and a leaked token is a live access path.

Every log attached to a vendor ticket or pasted into an AI chat widens the circle of people and jurisdictions that can read the original values. Good log analytics answers the question fast without creating a second incident.

A Short History of Log Analytics

Syslog, written by Eric Allman for Sendmail in the early 1980s, was later standardized in RFC 3164 (2001) and RFC 5424 (2009). For two decades, log analysis meant grep and awk on a central syslog server.

Windows went structured. Windows Vista replaced the legacy .evt format with the XML-based .evtx format and the channel model still used today, and Sysmon (2014) added high-fidelity process and network telemetry.

The mid-2000s brought SIEM. ArcSight, QRadar, and later Splunk made centralized search and correlation a product category, and ArcSight’s CEF is still emitted by most network appliances. The 2010s added open stacks such as ELK and cloud audit trails such as CloudTrail (2013).

In 2017, Sigma gave defenders a vendor-neutral rule format. The same year, SOC Prime began tagging Sigma rules with MITRE ATT&CK techniques and applied the approach to the public NotPetya investigation. ATT&CK mapping has since become a default expectation for detection content.

Where Log Analytics Is Heading

Detection moves upstream. Teams run Sigma rules on streaming events in the pipeline before data reaches the SIEM, cutting storage cost and shrinking mean time to detect from hours to minutes.

Correlation beats single alerts. Isolated low-fidelity matches are noise. Higher-order logic that links techniques across hosts and time windows into attack chains gives analysts something to confirm or close.

AI triage meets data-handling limits. LLMs explain process trees and summarize timelines well, but sending raw telemetry to a model provider raises privacy and contractual questions, and frontier models may refuse security content outright. During the July 2026 HuggingFace incident response, an attempt to send about 17,000 events to frontier models was blocked by guardrails.

Pseudonymization becomes a […]

title: How to Export Windows Event Logs (EVTX)
text:
The short answer: open Event Viewer, right-click the log you need (for example Windows Logs → Security), choose Save All Events As…, and keep the .evtx format. From an elevated command prompt, the same thing is one line: wevtutil epl Security C:\logs\security.evtx. Don’t copy the files out of C:\Windows\System32\winevt\Logs with Explorer. The Event Log service keeps them open, so you usually get an error or nothing usable.

EVTX is worth the extra minute compared with a text export. It’s the native format, so every field, the record IDs and the exact UTC timestamps survive. A SIEM can’t give you that back, because it stores rendered text. Prime Core has 11,632 sigma rules for Windows event logs, mapped to 643 MITRE ATT&CK techniques. They range from password guessing (T1110) and malicious services (T1543.003) to attackers clearing the logs behind them (T1070.001). Below is how to export the right logs, sanitize them, and investigate them for free in LogTotal.

Try LogTotal, free

TL;DR

RouteUse it whenWhat you needEvent Viewer → Save All Events AsOne machine, one or two logs, you have a desktop sessionAdmin rights, or Event Log Readers for most logswevtutil eplYou want a filtered export, a script, or a server without a GUIAn elevated promptwevtutil with /r: or a PowerShell loopSeveral logs, or a remote machineAdmin rights on the target, plus remote event log access through the firewall

Before you start

Three things decide whether the export contains what you hope it contains.

Rights. Administrators can export any log. Members of the local Event Log Readers group can read most logs without full admin. For the Security log, an elevated prompt is the dependable choice. Details are in our [Windows event log permissions guide].

Audit policy. Windows only logs what it’s told to. Process creation (event 4688) isn’t audited by default. Even when it is, the command line is recorded only if a separate policy is enabled. Check before you go looking for events that were never written:

auditpol /get /category:*

Log size and overwrite. Every log has a maximum size. By default, Windows overwrites the oldest events once the log is full, and on a busy server or domain controller that can mean only hours of history. See what you’re working with:

wevtutil gl Security

Look at maxSize and retention. If the attack happened before the oldest event in the log, it isn’t in there. Check your SIEM or forwarded events instead.

And the usual reminder: event logs are full of usernames, hostnames and IPs. LogTotal sanitizes uploads, but your data-handling policy still applies.

Which logs to export

“The Windows logs” is a few hundred channels on a modern system. For security work, these are the ones that usually carry the story:

Log (channel name)What it gives youNotesSecurityLogons (4624, 4625), account changes (4720, 4728), log cleared (1102), process creation (4688)4688 only if auditing is onSystemNew services (7045), service changes (7036), System log cleared (104)Microsoft-Windows-Sysmon/OperationalProcess creation with hashes and command lines, network connections, and moreOnly if Sysmon is installedMicrosoft-Windows-PowerShell/OperationalScript block logging (4104), the actual code that ranOnly if script block logging is enabledMicrosoft-Windows-Windows Defender/OperationalDetections (1116) and actions taken (1117)Microsoft-Windows-TaskScheduler/OperationalNew scheduled tasks (106), a favorite persistence trickMicrosoft-Windows-TerminalServices-LocalSessionManager/OperationalRDP session logon, disconnect, reconnect (21, 24, 25)

Not sure what a machine has? wevtutil el lists every channel. Pipe it through findstr /i sysmon (or whatever you’re hunting for) to check a specific one.

Option 1: Event Viewer

Best for one machine and a couple of logs.

Press Win+R, type eventvwr.msc, and run it as administrator.

Find the log. The classic ones are under Windows Logs. Everything else lives under Applications and Services Logs → Microsoft → […]

title: Where to Find SSH (sshd) Logs on Linux and How to Export Them
text:
On Debian and Ubuntu, sshd writes to /var/log/auth.log. On RHEL, Rocky, Alma and CentOS Stream, it writes to /var/log/secure. If neither file exists, your system logs only to the systemd journal. Then the command you want is journalctl -u ssh on Debian-based systems, or journalctl -u sshd on the Red Hat family, Fedora and Arch.

SSH is the front door of nearly every Linux server, which is why its logs show up in almost every Linux investigation. Prime Core has 11,632 sigma rules that run on Linux authentication logs like these, mapped to 643 MITRE ATT&CK techniques. Among them: brute force (T1110), logins with stolen credentials (T1078) and lateral movement over SSH (T1021.004). Below is how to find your sshd logs, export them, sanitize them, and investigate them for free in LogTotal.

Try LogTotal, free

TL;DR

Distro familyLog fileJournal commandDebian, Ubuntu/var/log/auth.logjournalctl -u sshRHEL, Rocky, Alma, CentOS Stream/var/log/securejournalctl -u sshdFedora, Arch, minimal installs without rsyslognone by defaultjournalctl -u sshd

Authentication logs are locked down on purpose, so a regular account usually gets nothing back.

/var/log/auth.log on Debian and Ubuntu is readable by root and the adm group.

/var/log/secure on the Red Hat family is root-only.

The system journal is open to root and to members of systemd-journal, adm and wheel. Everyone else sees only their own user journal. If you run journalctl -u ssh as a normal user, you get an empty result and a hint that you’re not seeing messages from other users. That’s permissions, not a quiet server.

The simple fix is sudo. If you’re setting up an account just for log collection, add it to adm or systemd-journal instead of handing out root. Our [Linux log permissions guide] covers the details.

One more thing before you copy anything off a server: auth logs contain usernames, source IPs and hostnames. LogTotal sanitizes uploads, but check your data-handling policy first.

Step 1: File, journal, or both?

The table above shows the defaults, and defaults are exactly what cloud images and hardening scripts like to change. Spend ten seconds checking:

ls -l /var/log/auth.log /var/log/secure 2>/dev/nullsystemctl is-active rsyslog

If a file shows up and rsyslog is active, you have both: rsyslog copies messages out of the journal into a plain text file. Either source works, and the file is easier to copy around.

If there’s no file, rsyslog simply isn’t installed. That’s the norm now: since Debian 12, rsyslog is no longer part of a default install, so a fresh Debian box has no auth.log at all. Fedora and Arch have worked this way for years. Go to Step 2b.

While you’re here, check whether the journal survives a reboot:

ls -d /var/log/journal

If that directory doesn’t exist, journald keeps logs in memory under /run/log/journal, and a reboot wipes them. On a machine you’re investigating, that’s worth knowing before anyone decides to “just restart it.”

One more point for incident work: if the box might be compromised, its local logs might be too. Wiping or editing auth.log is a classic cleanup step. If the server forwards logs to a SIEM, export from there as well and compare. Our [Splunk export guide] shows how.

Step 2a: Export from auth.log or secure

The current file only covers the last few days. Older entries sit in rotated files next to it. On Debian and Ubuntu they look like auth.log.1, auth.log.2.gz, and so on. On the Red Hat family they carry a date, like secure-20261012. If the incident started last week, you need those too.

This pulls sshd lines from the current and rotated files, oldest first, into one file:

zgrep reads plain and gzipped files alike, so you don’t have to unpack anything. ls -tr sorts by modification time, so the oldest file goes first and the output stays roughly […]

title: Log Analysis Tools: Key Features and 10 Top Picks
text:
En

LogTotal HOWTO

October 21, 2026
9 min read

Most investigations stall on a simple question: where are the logs, and how do I get them out? On Windows, event logs sit in %SystemRoot%\System32\winevt\Logs\ as binary .evtx files. Export them from Event Viewer (right-click a log, then Save All Events As…) or from an elevated prompt with wevtutil epl Security C:\IR\Security.evtx. On systemd-based Linux, the journal lives in /var/log/journal/ when persistent storage is enabled, or /run/log/journal/ when it is volatile, and journalctl -o json writes it out as one JSON object per line. Classic text syslog remains in /var/log/auth.log on Debian and Ubuntu, or /var/log/secure on RHEL-family hosts. Cloud and SaaS platforms expose their audit trails as JSON through the console or API.

Getting the file is the easy part. The hard part starts when a single host hands you 400,000 events, the clock is running, and legal wants to know who sees the raw data. This is where the top AI-driven log analytics tools separate from plain search consoles. Some apply machine-learning models on top of a SIEM. Others, like SOC Prime’s LogTotal, match every event against a precompiled detection library and return correlated attack chains, not a list of hits.

This guide covers what log analysis tools do, which features matter during incident response, ten tools worth knowing in 2026, and a step-by-step workflow for exporting Windows and Linux logs and investigating them in LogTotal. It closes with troubleshooting steps and answers to common questions.

Try LogTotal, free

What Are Log Analysis Tools?

Log analysis tools turn machine-generated records into answers: who acted, on which asset, when, from where, and through which mechanism. They parse raw formats, normalize fields, apply detection logic, and link related events so an analyst can reconstruct an intrusion instead of reading it line by line.

The category is broader than the SIEM. In a typical SOC, four kinds of tooling share the work:

SIEM and security analytics platforms (Splunk, Microsoft Sentinel, Google SecOps, Elastic) centralize ingestion, run scheduled and streaming detections, and handle triage and case management.

Security data pipelines (Cribl Stream, Fluent Bit, Vector) route, filter, and enrich events before storage, which controls ingestion cost and normalizes schemas such as ECS or OCSF.

DFIR utilities (Hayabusa, Chainsaw, EvtxECmd) process collected artifacts offline, usually EVTX, and produce timelines for a single host.

Snapshot analyzers such as LogTotal take an exported log set and return a full investigation without onboarding or integration work.

Log analysis is also distinct from log management. Management is plumbing: collection, retention, access control, integrity. Analysis is interpretation. A team can run a clean pipeline with 12 months of retention and still miss a Kerberoasting campaign if nothing evaluates the 4769 events with RC4 encryption type 0x17.

So what separates the best log analytics tools from the rest? Three things: how many formats they read without conversion, how much maintained detection content they apply, and whether they correlate isolated hits into an attack narrative. Speed and data-handling controls decide the rest, especially when the logs come from a host that was never onboarded to the SIEM.

Which Features Matter, and What Do They Buy You?

Feature lists on vendor pages look alike. During an incident, seven capabilities do most of the work.

Native parsers. EVTX is a chunked binary format with XML event payloads, so grep is useless against it. A tool should read EVTX, JSON/NDJSON, syslog (RFC 3164 and RFC 5424), and CEF without a conversion script.

Field normalization. A source IP should be the same field whether it came from a firewall, an IdP, or Sysmon Event ID 3. Schemas such as ECS and OCSF make one detection work across vendors.

title: CVE-2026-111943: Go Blocks Compromised eMudhra CA Keys After Certificate Authority Incident
text:
En

CVEs

October 21, 2026
9 min read

A major public key infrastructure incident has triggered emergency security measures across browsers, programming language ecosystems, certificate stores, and software packages. Private keys associated with eight eMudhra intermediate certificate authority certificates were compromised, potentially allowing unauthorized parties to create certificates that could appear trustworthy to vulnerable clients.

The incident affects six TLS intermediates used for domain-validated, organization-validated, and extended-validation certificates, along with two code-signing intermediates. Because an intermediate CA can issue certificates below a trusted root, possession of its private key creates a substantially different risk from the compromise of an ordinary website certificate. An attacker could potentially create fraudulent certificates that inherit trust from the affected chain.

The Go Project responded by introducing CVE-2026-111943, which addresses cases where Go applications could continue trusting certificate chains containing the compromised intermediates. Go 1.26.10 and 1.27.3 add a denylist to crypto/x509, causing certificate verification to fail when one of the known untrusted intermediate keys appears in a chain.

Security teams seeking CVE-2026-111943 detection opportunities should look beyond conventional vulnerability exploitation telemetry. This incident is fundamentally about certificate trust, so defenders should monitor TLS certificate chains, unexpected certificate issuers, certificate validation failures, suspicious encrypted sessions, and software that maintains its own certificate bundle rather than relying on rapidly updated browser revocation mechanisms.

Mozilla subsequently confirmed the compromise and, importantly, reported that its engineers were able to independently recover the affected private keys without receiving details about the researcher’s method. Mozilla concluded that the underlying key-generation process was flawed and straightforward to exploit.

The affected certificate authorities included:

The first six are TLS intermediates capable of participating in certificate chains used to authenticate websites. The remaining two are code-signing intermediates. title: CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619: Critical PHP RCE Flaws Trigger Emergency Security Release
text:
En

CVEs

October 21, 2026
8 min read

PHP administrators are facing an urgent security update after maintainers announced an out-of-cycle release addressing two critical vulnerabilities. The flaws, tracked by security researchers as CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619, have each received a CVSS v4.0 score of 9.2 from the PHP security team. Researchers at watchTowr describe both issues as remote code execution vulnerabilities.

The emergency release is scheduled for October 21, 2026, at 14:00 UTC. PHP moved the disclosure forward after information about the vulnerabilities reportedly leaked ahead of the coordinated release date. At the time of writing, PHP has not disclosed the vulnerable components, exploitation requirements, affected releases, or technical root causes and says those details will accompany the security updates.

Researchers have informally dubbed the vulnerability pair “PHP2Shell,” although this name does not come from the PHP Project. The early leak claimed the flaws could affect PHP releases dating back to PHP 5 and assigned them CVSS 10.0 scores. However, PHP’s official rating is 9.2, and the claimed version range has not yet been confirmed by an official vendor advisory.

The potential impact is nevertheless significant. PHP powers a massive number of websites, web applications, content management systems, e-commerce platforms, APIs, hosting panels, and custom enterprise services. If remote code execution is confirmed across commonly deployed configurations, successful exploitation could give attackers a direct route from an exposed web application to server-level compromise.

Security teams seeking CVE-2026-109618 detection opportunities should prioritize behavior-based monitoring while exploit-specific signatures remain unavailable. Suspicious activity includes PHP or web-server processes unexpectedly launching shells, interpreters, command-line utilities, or download tools.

title: LiteLLM 1.107.0 PyPI Wheel Contains a Credential Stealer and Persistent Python Backdoor
text:
Jump to sectionThe OpenSourceMalware team analyzed a wheel identifying itself as LiteLLM 1.107.0 and found a complete Python startup backdoor. The artifact does not merely contain suspicious strings or dormant test code: it installs two automatic execution paths, launches a credential-stealing payload, encrypts and uploads the results to www.litellm.dev, and creates a background process that retrieves and executes attacker-controlled Python every hour.The evidence supports treating this specific wheel as a malicious package compromise. Any system on which Python started after this wheel was installed should be considered potentially compromised.TL;DRThreat Type: PyPI supply-chain compromise, credential stealer, and persistent backdoorAffected Artifact: LiteLLM 1.107.0 macOS x86-64 wheel analyzed by OpenSourceMalwareImpact: Automatic execution on Python startup, credential collection, encrypted exfiltration, and unrestricted remote code executionPrimary C2: www.litellm.dev, which receives stolen data and appears to host an operator panel with victim informationExfiltration Endpoint: http://www.litellm.dev/healthcheckRemote Loader: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/letters9813/pythonclient-test/main/domain.txt followed by http://{domain}/codepyPersistence: Forked background process, lock file, suppressed output, and hourly C2 pollingWheel SHA-256: 7598727f209d717041db37f7dca271d3a7d328a279890e0e1d55375729aeb86dContextUpwind’s security research team publicly reported the compromise on October 21, 2026. They found that all seven LiteLLM 1.107.0 wheels on PyPI contain the same three injected files, and that the payload is absent from the v1.107.0 git tag. The payload file hashes in our sample match the RECORD values in Upwind’s report, and the wheel hash matches their entry for the macOS x86-64 wheel. How the build environment or publishing credential was compromised remains unknown.This is the second compromise of LiteLLM on PyPI in 2026. In March, versions 1.82.7 and 1.82.8 were published using a PyPI token stolen during TeamPCP’s Trivy supply chain attack. Both incidents use Python startup hooks in tampered wheels, but the infrastructure differs. We are not attributing the October compromise to TeamPCP or any other actor.DiscoveryThe wheel contains three files that should not appear in a legitimate LiteLLM installation:FilePurposeSHA-256cook.pthExecutes import cook during Python startup7f191632e7320705d154b85204f1ae546b543acbd7e8861229b76f5042b92bdbcook.pyDecodes and runs a credential-stealing payload9dd0a3926f96a37eb86cf1ee2310d9be93139cc4ebef3ef9e2efe9531390be25sitecustomize.pyContains a stealer variant and runs the persistent remote-code loader34bef04fe88ac9d0aae0475630b1738681d15b94f233ac8aa46eacf5968305faThe files are listed with valid hashes in the wheel’s RECORD manifest. We verified all 3,946 hashed entries in that manifest and found no mismatches. This is important: the malicious files were incorporated into the packaged artifact and its integrity metadata rather than appended to the unpacked directory afterward.The analyzed wheel is:Filename: litellm-1.107.0-cp310-abi3-macosx_10_12_x86_64.whl
Size: 38,106,866 bytes
SHA-256: 7598727f209d717041db37f7dca271d3a7d328a279890e0e1d55375729aeb86d
Automatic Execution on Python StartupThe first execution mechanism is a 12-byte .pth file:import cook
Python processes executable import lines in .pth files while initializing site-packages. An application does not need to import LiteLLM for this code to run. Starting Python in an environment containing the installed wheel is sufficient.The imported cook.py file is a single obfuscated statement. exec(zlib.decompress(base64.b64decode("...")))

More and More Cyber Jobs Require AI Expertise
But There's No Consensus Way to Assess Levels of Skill

A growing number of cybersecurity jobs require not just a baseline familiarity with AI tools, but significant AI expertise, according to an analysis of validated job vacancies in the field.See Also: OnDemand | Shorter Certificates, Higher Risk: What Security Teams Must Do Now
"We're mapping this stuff in real time and using real data," said Rob T. Lee, chief AI officer and chief of research at the Sans Institute, a training and certification organization. Lee said he gathered data through application programming interfaces on job sites using an artificial intelligence agent, not through web-scraping, which means job postings could be validated individually. The data comprises a two-day job market snapshot of 6,193 active postings taken from Sept. 15 to Sept. 17.
The methodology produces reliable, accurate data, which can be analyzed to show trends over time, Lee told ISMG. "It won't tell you the total number of AI cybersecurity jobs that are out there … but it is a good sample to be able to do trend analysis" because it is basically looking at the same data set over and over again, as it changes over time.
Sans found employers are already hiring four types of AI-heavy positions: AI/ML Security Engineer, AI Security Architect, AI Governance and Security Risk Lead and AI Red Team Engineer.
"These roles are probably going to be needed by every organization that's out there. I just can't see anyone who's pulling an AI into their organization feeling comfortable that cybersecurity engineering is not a key part of that," Lee explained.
Lee also identified four roles the report lists as "building," with fewer postings and hiring typically being done under non-AI related titles, but a growing proportion of the role focused on AI issues. These are: Agentic AI Security Engineer, AI Security Operations Center Orchestrator, AI Incident Response Orchestrator and AI Threat Intelligence Analyst.
An orchestrator is a coder who manages and directs a fleet or swarm of AI agents. Agents are AI programs that don't just chat with users but can interact with company applications and perform functions. These jobs would become more common next year, as SOCs and cyber defense teams figured out how to use AI agents in their workflows, Lee said.
The tally of 1,654 AI-focused vacancies comes not from looking at the job title alone, but analyzing the content of the posting and the skills required, said Lee.
The hiring companies included some of the nation's largest corporations including JP Morgan Chase, Leidos, Amazon, Mastercard and PepsiCo. "This isn't cybersecurity firms doing these hires. You've got the energy sector, healthcare, oil and gas," Lee said.
"This year I actually think that AI is going to have new roles on the cybersecurity side of these organizations," Lee said. "Just like with ICS and OT, you need specific expertise in this field," he said, referring to industrial control systems and operational technology."
Sans has posted the data online and pledged to update it regularly.
Kee said the data collected so far undermines the narrative that AI will replace humans in cybersecurity. Instead, he argued, it will augment them.
"The analogy I like to use is, you could swim through a pool, but if you put flippers on, you're going to be able to swim it faster. That's what AI is going to enable you to do, but you're still hiring a swimmer."
And, despite the growing number of AI-specialist jobs, the predicted drop off in entry level openings as those positions were replaced by AI hasn't materialized either, Lee added.
"We're not seeing a downward curve on the entry-level jobs in cybersecurity either. […]

A post from the independent risk research institute reviewed Anthropic's last annual risk assessment, which tracked potential risks emanating from frontier models. Metr said it agrees with Anthropic's determination that the risk of catastrophic harm from its models is low – but said that's not because of the frontier lab has strict guardrails, but because models' currently lack the ability for to cause a catastrophe.

The review, which Metr undertook without the "employee-level" access Anthropic bestowed on it earlier this month, included several risk-reduction recommendations. Metr conducted the review specifically for the AI lab's August 2026 Risk Report.

The evaluator said the review occurred before that agreement and falls outside the timeframe it agreed to cover. Metr said Anthropic shared an initial draft of the August risk report in July and compared it to the version published on August 14.

"We are not confident that, if risk were higher, the methodology in the report would reliably identify this," Metr said in its post.

It added that a stronger assertion that Anthropic models are not misaligned "would need much more extensive empirical work and would require solving multiple open scientific problems" that Metr researchers believe will be challenging given the pace of development.
Metr said recent incidents in any case undermine Anthropic's arguments. It pointed to Anthropic changing its risk assessment from "very low" in the first draft to "low" without changing the report's content. The revision came about because of incidents involving both models the report examined.

Metr recommended that Anthropic establish more comprehensive red-teaming of its monitoring system and include potential risks from models currently being trained.

The evaluator said Anthropic's monitoring system "failed to catch previous incidents and has several limitations that undermine its reliability." Expanded red-teaming of the monitoring system needs to include deliberate testing of worst-case inputs and measure how often AI agents try to tamper with or lie to the monitor.

Third-party evaluators like Metr have become more prominent in recent months after the Hugging Face incident in which OpenAI agents hacked the model repository. Since then, concerns about AI safety have grown, and AI CEOs, most vocally Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei, have supported calls to slow AI development.

Prakash Panjwani, CEO, Acronis (Image: Acronis)

Acronis snagged longtime WatchGuard leader Prakash Panjwani as its next chief executive to help managed service providers consolidate their cyber spend with fewer vendors.See Also: Norlem claims "unfair advantage" for its SOC and clients from unified Cortex platform
The Schaffhausen, Switzerland-based company plans to capitalize on its heritage around backup, disaster recovery and cyber resilience as it pushes more into pure cyber markets including MDR and XDR, Panjwani said. Acronis' true differentiation in MDR and XDR relies on the firm's open telemetry ingestion and AI-driven automated remediation rather than closed proprietary ecosystems, he said.
"MDR is truly about telemetry," Panjwani told ISMG. "How much data do you collect, and how quickly can you remediate after you have that information? The best MDR players have to be the ones who are, over time, the most open."
Panjwani joined Acronis after spending more than a decade as CEO of SMB-focused cybersecurity provider WatchGuard, which he helped the company expand beyond network firewalls to a broader MSP cybersecurity platform through a series of acquisitions. He replaces Jan-Jaap Jager, who had led Acronis since November 2025 and will remain a company shareholder (see: Securing Data With Immutable Backups and Automated Recovery).
How Panjwani Plans to Make Acronis More MSP-Friendly
MSPs increasingly seek vendor consolidation to avoid managing dozens of disparate dashboards, and Panjwani said Acronis has a distinct edge because of its financial scale, a proprietary ground-up designed architecture that avoids disjointed acquired interfaces, and an open API approach that integrates telemetry and third-party tools. He said MSPs value open integrations and remediation to combat AI and SaaS sprawl.
"I just believe that over time there'll be a lot more consolidation around that MSP space and into platforms, and I just think that Acronis' size and the spread of the MSP space sets it up for being the consolidator in the space," Panjwani said.
The biggest bottleneck for MSPs is technician capacity, but by designing automation from the ground up for MSP technicians, Panjwani said Acronis frees significant operational bandwidth for MSPs to acquire new clients. Automating routine technician workflows by up to 80% frees MSPs to expand services, he said.
"If you can build with that technician persona in mind, you're able to automate the little tasks, everything they do," Panjwani said. "If they show up in the morning, they have a list of tasks to go through. If we automated all of those things, we'd shrink that list by 80%. Imagine what they can do with their time."
Growth vectors include expanding within Acronis' 21,000 MSPs, increasing adoption of existing services, and moving into adjacent areas such as MDR/XDR through automated remediation and open telemetry ingestion, Panjwani said. He said Acronis occupies a strategic middle ground, providing both internal MSP operational automation as well as end-user security and resilience.
"When I look at the Acronis platform, it's truly built ground up, which allows us to have more functionality that's fully automated for the MSP," Panjwani said. "As we add more things to the platform, it's about maintaining that element."
How Panjwani Plans to Spend His First Months at Acronis

title: PHP Foundation Says Chainguard Broke Security Embargo Ahead of Emergency Patches
text: BackSecurity NewsPHP Foundation Says Chainguard Broke Security Embargo Ahead of Emergency PatchesThe PHP Foundation says Chainguard broke a security embargo ahead of critical RCE patches, as leaks disrupted the coordinated release.Sarah GoodingOct 21, 2026|6 min read The PHP Foundation says Chainguard broke a coordinated security embargo by releasing patched PHP container images hours ahead of schedule, making the fix available for attackers to study while other distributors were still preparing updates.In a postmortem published October 21, the Foundation described a disclosure process disrupted by leaked CVE identifiers, an accidentally published exploit demonstration, and Chainguard’s decision to release early. It also acknowledged that work on the underlying memory management problem had stalled repeatedly after developers first noticed signs of it in 2024.The account follows PHP’s emergency patches for two critical remote code execution vulnerabilities, CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619. Researchers demonstrated attacks that could execute code on web servers without logging in. The PHP Foundation wrote:On October 21st at 07:41 UTC, more than six hours before the coordinated release, Chainguard unilaterally broke the embargo and published built images containing the fix. Like other distributors, Chainguard had received the patch in advance so its users could update the moment the vulnerabilities were disclosed. Any attacker could now study the fix in binary form while every other PHP user was still waiting for the release. This disregarded weeks of work by many parties toward a coordinated disclosure.Chainguard CEO Dan Lorenc described the decision in a Hacker News comment posted earlier that day.“I made the call to get these out early when exploits hit in the wild,” Lorenc wrote. He praised the maintainers’ work, said Chainguard had extensively tested the patch, and said the images were free and would remain so.In a subsequent LinkedIn post, Lorenc defended his decision and apologized for the additional stress on PHP’s maintainers.Lorenc said Chainguard independently discovered the vulnerability after receiving an initial warning on Friday, using its testing harness and a frontier AI model, and later helped test the fixes. By Tuesday night, he said, several other security vendors involved in the disclosure had reported exploits in the wild.“After talking to several of the other researchers on a video call, I made the call to ship the fixes and immediately notified the group,” Lorenc wrote.He cited those exploitation reports, the ease of independently discovering and exploiting the vulnerability, and information already circulating publicly as reasons for releasing early. He said the patched artifacts were publicly accessible to everyone, including organizations that were not Chainguard customers.The Foundation offered a narrower assessment of the exploit code circulating before disclosure. Its security team inspected public proof-of-concept exploits after the leak but had not identified any functional ones by release time.Lorenc did not name the vendors or publish supporting evidence of exploitation in his post. The Foundation’s assessment of the public PoCs it examined does not rule out exploitation elsewhere.Cloudflare’s Dane Knecht had also reported early attacks before the patches arrived and said the company had deployed temporary WAF protections. His warning did not establish that those attacks had successfully compromised servers. Lorenc has previously argued that embargoes are essential to protecting users before vulnerability details become public. In his July 5 post, Summer of Clearinghouses, he explained how a published fix can help attackers locate the underlying vulnerability.“Pre-disclosure protection extends exactly as far as the people you can vet and hold to an embargo,” he wrote.Chainguard’s vulnerability disclosure policy, last updated September 22, says the company may shorten disclosure timelines in […]
