Utah has approved three more healthcare AI pilots for its "AI regulatory sandbox," including projects for medication prescriptions, refills, and physical therapy. (Image: Getty Images)

The state of Utah has given the green light for three more healthcare technology companies to test how their artificial intelligence systems can safely provide services such as prescribing and refilling medications and providing AI-augmented physical therapy plans for specific health conditions.See Also: Webinar | Verifying AI Agent Activity Against Your Data Policies
The separate pilot projects, involving Magic Health, Inc., which does business as Nolla Health, August AI Labs and Expect Fitness, are part of Utah's AI Regulatory Sandbox, which provides limited regulatory relief to companies testing AI technologies under state supervision.
Two of the experiments focus on prescriptions, from Nolla Health's AI-assessed and generated prescriptions for acne cream and gel medications for adults to August AI Lab's pilot for prescription renewals of existing maintenance medications for patients already on established treatment plans. Expect Fitness' application creates AI-developed physical therapy treatment plans for women with pelvic floor disorders such as incontinence.
The Utah Legislature established its AI Regulatory Sandbox in May 2024 to gather data and advise the state on how to AI-based applications in healthcare, a spokesperson of Utah's office of AI told ISMG.
"The sandbox provides a controlled, supervised environment to evaluate innovative AI tools while giving the Legislature the data needed to make evidence-based policy updates," she said.
The AI pilot agreements establish phased testing requirements, clinical oversight, escalation procedures and regulatory reporting aimed at helping Utah evaluate the safety and effectiveness of the technologies.
The agreements also require the pilot companies to implement "reasonable cybersecurity protections against data leaks to minimize the risk of breach of confidential information," including best practices to address emerging threats and vulnerabilities.
The companies also must "possess and continuously maintain professional liability insurance coverage throughout the duration of their state agreements," the state said.
"Our office enforces a strict governance framework featuring stage-gated rollouts that require 100% human clinician review during initial phases before any system can earn broader autonomy," the AI office spokesperson told ISMG.
For healthcare pilots, "we require specialized malpractice insurance and 24-hour adverse event reporting. We also recently contracted third-party technical and clinical auditing firms to independently verify decision logs and stress-test system guardrails for authorized pilots," the spokesperson said.
The new test projects are among several other healthcare-related AI pilots Utah has authorized for the regulatory sandbox since 2024.
Others included a pilot launched in January by New York-based telehealth provider Doctronic that Utah dubbed as the nation's first state-approved program to legally prescribe routine refills using an autonomous AI health platform (see: Utah Moves Ahead with AI-Powered Rx Refills Despite Pushback).
Utah allowed the Doctronic pilot project to forge ahead earlier this year with some concessions to appease various safety concerns by the states' medical licensing board.

text:

US, UK and Germany Warn of Active SafePay Ransomware
Vertically Integrated Double-Extortion Group Hacks 13 Victims in 12 Days

Tiffany Wang •
October 21, 2026

$('.fa.fa-print').click(function () {
window.print();
});

Since August 2024, SafePay has compromised at least 600 victims across multiple critical infrastructure sectors. (Image: Shutterstock)

A double-extortion group called SafePay has been actively targeting businesses and critical infrastructure worldwide, according to a joint cybersecurity advisory from U.S., U.K. and German government agencies.See Also: OnDemand | Beyond Point Solutions: Securing AI Coding, Models, and Runtime Environments
Since August 2024, SafePay has compromised at least 600 victims across multiple critical infrastructure sectors, the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency said Tuesday. The financially motivated campaigns are characterized by data theft followed by swift encryption of victim systems within 24 hours.
The ransomware group posted 13 breaches in the first 12 days of October on its data leak site, with victims including a U.S. biotechnology firm to a Swiss hotel and a German construction company.
Despite the prolific attacks, SafePay maintains a low profile by operating independently throughout its ransomware campaigns. The group handles initial access, deployment and extortion in house rather than renting its malware to affiliates like most ransomware-as-a-service operators, said threat intelligence firm Huntress.
SafePay's ransomware binary overlaps with the leaked LockBit Black source code, Huntress said, sharing command-line flags and encryption logic with the ransomware builder that has enabled numerous new variants since 2022.
"SafePay has added its own features on top, including a Cyrillic language kill switch that stops the malware from running on systems set to Eastern European languages," Huntress said.
Many cybersecurity firms suspect SafePay is based in Russia. "The group does not allow targeting of Commonwealth of Independent States," said U.K.-based Quorum Cyber. "This is commonly a trait of groups based within Russia."
The group gains initial access through compromised credentials, brute-force password attacks and exploitation of VPN vulnerabilities, the Federal Bureau of Investigation, U.S. Secret Service and Germany's Landeskriminalamt Rheinland-Pfalz reported.
SafePay actors route their connections through commercial VPN service Mullvad to conceal their actual IP addresses when accessing victim networks and rely on accounts stolen from phishing to authenticate.
To gain initial access, they exploit edge device flaws in Cisco security software Adaptive Security Appliance and Firepower Threat Defense that provide firewall and VPN services. One vulnerability, tracked as CVE-2020-3259, could allow attackers to retrieve sensitive information from an affected devices' memory. The other flaw, assigned CVE-2023-20269, could allow unauthorized users to establish clientless SSL VPN sessions.
The agencies also found SafePay exploiting two vulnerabilities in data backup software Veeam. One flaw, tracked as CVE-2023-27532, could allow attackers to obtain encrypted credentials from the configuration database and gain access to backup infrastructure hosts. The other one, cataloged as CVE-2024-40711, is a high-severity deserialization vulnerability that could allow remote code execution.
Another vulnerability in firewall and VPN provider SonicWall, assigned CVE-2024-40766, is also used to gain unauthorized access.
"After SafePay threat actors gain access to a victim network, they establish persistence by gaining administrative privileges on existing accounts, or on newly created accounts, using built-in administrative tools consistent with living off the land techniques," CISA said.
The group uses legitimate Windows administration tools, including PsExec and Windows Remote Management, to […]

title: Digital Arts, maker of the i-FILTER web filtering and m-FILTER email security products used across Japanese companies, government and schools, says stolen operations credentials let intruders into the environment running six cloud services. Some traces date back to July 2025.An AI-assisted review on Oct 9 found what earlier checks missed. When the security vendor is the way in, review your filter policies, not just passwords.https://japancyberwatch.com/articles/digital-arts-security-vendor-breach-cloud-services-2026#infosec #SupplyChain #Japan
text:
Key takeaways

Digital Arts (デジタルアーツ), a Tokyo-listed security company whose i-FILTER web filtering and m-FILTER email security products are among the most widely used in Japanese companies, government bodies and schools, said on October 21, 2026 that attackers had been inside the environment it uses to run its cloud services.
The attackers used stolen credentials meant for operating those services. Some of the traces date back to around July 2025, about 15 months earlier.
Information on some customers of six cloud services, including i-FILTER@Cloud and m-FILTER@Cloud, may have been viewed. Digital Arts has found no sign that it was taken out. It also found traces in its internal environment.
It found the intrusion on October 9 during an AI-assisted review of its systems, products and internal environment, prompted by the recent wave of attacks in Japan. Earlier checks had missed it.
All customers of the six services are asked to change administrator and user passwords. Versions of the products installed on customers' own systems are not affected.

What Digital Arts disclosed#

How it was found
An AI-assisted review of systems, products and the internal environment on October 9, which found traces "that earlier checks had not found"

How long
Some traces date back to around July 2025

Where
The operating environment of its cloud services, and its internal environment

How
Credentials used to operate the cloud services were obtained by a third party and used to get in. How they were stolen is not stated

Customer impact
Information on some customers of the services below may have been viewed. No exfiltration confirmed, and no misuse reported, as of noon on October 21

Response
Stolen credentials invalidated; its own operations credentials replaced; suspicious programs stopped; server authentication keys replaced. No new access seen since. It is also rebuilding its services and network

Business impact
Under review

The six services:

Service
What it does

i-FILTER@Cloud
Cloud version of i-FILTER web filtering

m-FILTER@Cloud (Modern Edition)
Cloud email security and filtering

m-FILTER MailAdviser for Microsoft 365
Email add-on for Microsoft 365

FINAL CODE@Cloud
File encryption and tracking

Z-FILTER
Combined secure web access (SSE) and identity (IDaaS) service

Desk
Cloud service (not described in the notice)

Digital Arts asks all customers of these services to change both administrator and user passwords, and will contact some customers about further steps. Customers who run the software versions on their own servers are not affected.
What we don't know yet#
Digital Arts has not said:

How the operations credentials were stolen
What customer information sits in the affected environment: settings, user lists, logs of web or email traffic, files, or something else
How many customers are affected
What the "suspicious programs" it stopped were, and whether attackers could change how the services behaved, not only read data
How the intrusion into its internal environment relates to the cloud one, and whether any systems that the on-premises products connect to, such as for updates, were reachable from it. Digital Arts says the on-premises versions are not affected
What its AI-assisted review looked at, and why earlier checks missed what it found

Our analysis#
When the security vendor is the way in#
In our experience, the on-premises versions of i-FILTER and m-FILTER are among the most common security products in Japanese organizations, from companies to local governments and schools. Digital Arts last published a market share figure in 2015, when it cited an ITR survey putting i-FILTER at 48% of Japan's URL filtering market. How many organizations use the cloud versions affected here is not public, and the on-premises products are not affected. But the name alone means many Japanese security teams will be asking whether they are exposed.

PrintHomeNewsArticleArizona's IMS Care Center Discloses Breach of Patient DataArticlesIMS Care Center Discloses Patient Data Breach from Email SystemArizona's IMS Care Center Discloses Breach of Patient Data MEDIUMOctober 21, 20263m readData BreachPhishingRegulatory STIX 2.1 Viz Sigma Related Entities Other IMS Care Center, LLCCyberscoutTransUnion MITRE ATT&CK Techniques T1566Initial AccessPhishingT1078Initial AccessValid AccountsT1114.002CollectionRemote Email Collection Full Report Export Markdown Executive Summary
IMS Care Center, LLC, a large multispecialty medical group based in Phoenix, Arizona, has reported a data breach that exposed the personal and protected health information (PHI) of its patients. According to a notification filed with the New Hampshire Attorney General on October 16, 2026, the breach resulted from an unauthorized party gaining access to the company's corporate email environment. The incident occurred in June 2026, and a subsequent investigation confirmed that sensitive data, including Social Security numbers and medical information, may have been compromised. IMS Care Center is now in the process of notifying affected individuals and has begun offering identity theft protection services.
Incident Overview
The timeline of the incident is as follows:

June 17-18, 2026: An unauthorized party gained access to certain accounts within IMS Care Center's corporate email system.
June 18, 2026: The company detected the unusual activity and immediately launched an investigation with the assistance of external cybersecurity experts.
September 30, 2026: A lengthy and detailed review of the affected email accounts was completed. This review identified the specific types of data that were potentially exposed.
October 16, 2026: IMS Care Center began mailing notification letters to individuals whose information was identified in the compromised accounts.

The attack vector appears to be a compromise of the email environment, which is a common target in the healthcare industry, often resulting from successful phishing campaigns or credential theft.
Data Exposed
The investigation determined that the compromised email accounts contained a wide range of sensitive patient information. The types of data exposed could include:

Personal Identifiers: Full Name, Address
Social Security Numbers (SSNs)
Protected Health Information (PHI): Medical information, which could include diagnoses, treatment details, and patient history.

The exposure of both SSNs and PHI makes this a particularly serious breach, as it puts affected individuals at risk of both financial identity theft and other malicious activities.
Response Actions
In response to the breach, IMS Care Center has taken several steps:

Investigation: Engaged third-party cybersecurity professionals to investigate the scope and nature of the incident.
Security Enhancements: The company reports that it is reviewing its existing policies and procedures and implementing additional security measures to prevent future incidents.
Notification: Notifying relevant regulatory bodies (such as state Attorneys General) and affected individuals as required by law.
Support for Victims: Offering 12 months of complimentary credit monitoring and identity theft restoration services through Cyberscout (a TransUnion service).

Impact on Individuals
Individuals affected by this data breach face a significant risk of harm. With their names, SSNs, and medical information exposed, they are vulnerable to:

Identity Theft: Criminals can use SSNs to open new lines of credit, file fraudulent tax returns, or apply for benefits.
Medical Identity Theft: Malicious actors could use stolen medical information to receive medical care, purchase prescription drugs, or submit fraudulent claims to insurance providers.
Targeted Phishing: The stolen data could be used to craft highly convincing phishing scams targeting the victims.

title: 🛡 THREAT INTEL | police.rajasthan.gov.in🟢 Actor "Scarlettgroup" claims Undisclosed⚠️ Unverified claimhttps://www.yazoul.net/intel/claim/2026-10-21-rajasthan-police-ransomware-claim-by-scarlettgroup-oct-2026by Yazoul AI#DarkWeb #DataBreach #ThreatIntel #CyberSecurity #InfoSec
text:
Unverified dark web claim. This report is based on a post observed on a dark web forum. Yazoul Security has not independently verified the authenticity of this claim.
Leak Site Screenshot Screenshot captured at time of discovery. Image blurred to protect victim PII. × Claim Summary
The ransomware group known as Scarlettgroup has allegedly listed police.rajasthan.gov.in, the official domain of the Rajasthan Police, on its leak site. According to the threat actor, the attack date is recorded as October 14, 2026. The group claims to have exfiltrated data belonging to the Rajasthan Police, which it describes as the state law enforcement agency responsible for maintaining law and order, preventing crime, and protecting citizens across Rajasthan, India.
The claimed data volume is listed as undisclosed. No samples, file listings, or proof-of-compromise artifacts have been publicly corroborated at the time of writing. This report treats the claim as unverified and speculative. The listing appears in the Government & Defense sector, a category that ransomware operators frequently target for both financial and reputational leverage.
Threat Actor Profile
Scarlettgroup is a relatively obscure ransomware operation with limited publicly available intelligence. At the time of this writing, there is no confirmed count of total known victims, no documented toolset, and no peer-reviewed or vendor research references available. This absence of a track record is itself a significant analytical caveat.
Because the group’s known tools and tactics are unknown, defenders should not assume a specific initial access vector, encryption family, or exfiltration method. Common ransomware tradecraft - including phishing, exposed remote access services, and exploitation of unpatched internet-facing systems - remains plausible but unconfirmed for this actor. Organizations should treat Scarlettgroup as an unknown-quantity threat and apply baseline hardening rather than actor-specific countermeasures. No public YARA rules or detection signatures specific to Scarlettgroup are currently available; generic ransomware behavioral detections and endpoint monitoring remain the practical guidance.
Alleged Data Exposure
The threat actor claims to hold data from the Rajasthan Police, but the volume, format, and sensitivity of any purported data remain undisclosed. No samples have been published or independently reviewed. It is important to note that ransomware groups routinely exaggerate the scope and sensitivity of stolen data to pressure victims into payment. Claims involving law enforcement agencies are especially prone to inflation, given the perceived leverage of citizen data.
Yazoul Security has not accessed, downloaded, or reviewed any leaked material, and this report intentionally omits any links, samples, or access details.
Potential Impact
If the claim is accurate, potential impact could include exposure of internal communications, operational records, or citizen-adjacent information held by a state police agency. Such exposure could carry privacy, regulatory, and public trust implications. However, none of this is confirmed. The absence of a disclosed data volume makes impact assessment highly speculative. Downstream risks such as credential reuse, targeted phishing, or secondary extortion are theoretical at this stage.
What to Watch For

Official statements from Rajasthan Police or Indian government authorities confirming or denying the incident.
Publication of verifiable proof-of-compromise artifacts by the threat actor.
Appearance of the listing on additional aggregator sites or cross-posting by affiliated groups.
Any observed use of stolen data in follow-on phishing or fraud campaigns.
Updates to our actor profile at /intel/actor/scarlettgroup/ as new intelligence emerges.

text:
The Mailbag
The patches arrived this afternoon. The exploits were already there.

TP

The Perimeter Desk
The Mailbag

2026-10-21

# The patches arrived this afternoon. The exploits were already there.

My inbox looks exactly like the rest of the internet right now. It's full of panic from people who are a bit late to the party. Most folks are looking at PHP2Shell and wondering why their house is burning down when the sprinklers just started running.

I don't use words like "critical" often. Marketing teams love that word because it helps them sell you a more expensive subscription. But CVE-2026-109618 has a CVSS score of 9.4. That isn't some polite hint. It's a scream. Why would you try to "manage risk" when remote code execution is sitting in the core of a language that runs a huge part of the web, especially since the flaws leaked before the patches were ready? You scramble.

Here is the mailbag for Wednesday 21 October 2026.

**Gary, Des Moines: "I run a small bakery with a simple WordPress site. Do I really need to worry about this 'PHP2Shell' thing? We aren't exactly a target for hackers."**

Gary, I appreciate the optimism, but attackers aren't looking for your sourdough recipes. They’re looking for any server running an unpatched version of PHP that they can turn into a botnet node or a pivot point into something larger.

If you're using a managed hosting provider, they've likely already applied the emergency patches released this afternoon. If you're managing your own VPS, you are currently exposed. The beauty of an RCE is that it doesn't require a targeted attack; it just requires a script scanning the entire IPv4 space for a vulnerability. In the eyes of an automated exploit kit, your bakery is identical to a mid-sized accounting firm. Update your PHP version immediately.

**Lin, Singapore: "The official advisory for CVE-2026-109618 lists it as critical, but I'm reading some researcher writeups suggesting the actual impact depends on specific server configurations. Who is right?"**

This is where things get interesting. The vendor sees a theoretical maximum—full server control—and assigns a 9.4. Researchers are looking at the prerequisite conditions and saying "it's complicated."

I'm sticking with the version numbers. Once an exploit hits the web before the official patch comes out, the theoretical stuff becomes real fast. You can't wait around for some consensus between a vendor advisory and a blog post to decide if it's time to move. If you do that, you've missed your chance. Why wait? Hundreds of websites went offline today, which suggests anyone who paused for nuance is now staring at 404 errors.

**Sarah, Sacramento: "My daughter is in public school here. I saw the news about the ETS breach and California warning students. What exactly was stolen?"**

The specifics are still surfacing, but we know it involves sensitive data for millions of students. The real issue here isn't just what was taken, but how it happened.

ETS was a contractor. The school didn't fail your daughter. The vendor they trusted did. This is how the modern supply chain works. We hand our data over to specialists to cut costs, but we're just moving the risk to some third party that handles thousands of other clients. Why do this? It makes things easy for criminals. If an attacker hits one contractor like ETS, they don't have to hunt for a single school. They get student records for an entire state in one shot.

***

The PHP2Shell disaster highlights a recurring failure in the disclosure cycle. We are still pretending that "responsible disclosure" works in an era where exploit code leaks faster than a vendor can write a regression test. The emergency patches released this afternoon are technically sound, but they are late.

Some will argue that WAFs and perimeter defenses should have caught this. That's a fantasy. A WAF is a band-aid on a broken leg; it might stop the bleeding for a minute, but the bone is still snapped. When the flaw is in […]

title: ⚠️ PATCH NOWTwo critical PHP core flaws (CVE-2026-109618/619, CVSS 9.2) leaked before the patch shipped.A public proof-of-concept is circulating. The emergency fix covers PHP 8.2 to 8.5.Running PHP? Update the moment it drops.https://suriq.io/blog/php-core-rce-cve-2026-109618-php2shell#CVE #DataBreach #infosec #cybersecurity
text:
Home/ Blog/ Security news/ Article Blog · Security news PHP CVE-2026-109618: Critical RCE Leaked, Patch Immediately PHP 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36 and 8.2.35 fix two critical CVSS 9.2 core flaws, CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619, that leaked before release. Update now. By Suriq's Jack · Oct 21, 2026 · 13:24 UTC ·Security news · 5 min read · Updated Oct 21, 2026
Mitigate now↓ Update, October 21, 13:45 UTC: PHP released the fix early, around 00:30 UTC on October 21, in PHP 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36 and 8.2.35. An earlier version of this post described the release as still pending and said a public proof-of-concept was circulating. Huntress reports no public exploit code, only a short video that was posted and removed, so we have corrected both.
On October 20, 2026, the PHP security team posted an unusual advance notice: an emergency release for two critical vulnerabilities in PHP core, both rated CVSS version 4.0 9.2, scheduled for Wednesday, October 21 at 14:00 UTC. Tracked as CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619, the flaws are serious enough that PHP broke its normal pattern and warned the world a day early, reserving the right to ship sooner if details went public or exploitation appeared. Details went public: researchers nicknamed the flaws php2shell, and the SANS Internet Storm Center raised its InfoCon to yellow. PHP did ship sooner: PHP 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36 and 8.2.35 landed around 00:30 UTC on October 21.
PHP runs a large share of the web, so a flaw in its core is not a single-vendor problem. It is a problem for nearly everyone who operates a web server. That is exactly why this one deserves a clear-eyed read rather than a panic, and the first job is to separate what PHP has actually confirmed from what is being reported around it.
What PHP has confirmed, and what it has not
The official PHP advisory is short. It confirms that PHP 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36 and 8.2.35 fix two vulnerabilities that can allow unauthenticated remote code execution, that both are rated CVSS v4.0 9.2, and that "there are no complete mitigations, updating is the only safe choice."
Everything beyond that is reported, not official. watchTowr notes leaked claims that the flaw reaches back as far as PHP 5, while cautioning that no vendor advisory has confirmed the scope or the root cause. Huntress says the vulnerable component remains unidentified. Early community analysis has pointed at PHP's handling of multipart form uploads, but that too is unconfirmed. Treat the older-version claims and the root cause as unconfirmed until PHP publishes the technical details.
What is not in dispute: fixes ship only for the supported branches, PHP 8.2 through 8.5, as 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36 and 8.2.35. Anything on 8.1 or older is end of life and will not receive a patch, and PHP 8.2 itself reaches end of life on December 31, 2026. If you are still running an EOL branch, the only real fix is to move forward.
Why a PHP core flaw hits hosting operators harder
Most critical CVEs we cover affect one product you can inventory and gate. PHP is different because it is a dependency of almost everything on a typical web host: WordPress, Magento and other storefronts, Laravel and Symfony apps, control-panel tooling, and countless bespoke sites all sit on the same interpreter. A single server can run several PHP versions at once through per-site handlers, which means the exposure is not one box to patch but a matrix of sites and versions to walk. Command injection and remote code execution already rank second only to cross-site scripting among the bug classes we logged across the events we triaged in the last 90 days, and a flaw in the runtime beneath all of those applications is the broadest version of that pattern.
The practical consequence is that "update PHP" is rarely one action on a real host. It is an update per branch, per site handler, with an application-compatibility check behind each. Walk that inventory today, branch by branch.
What to do now that the patch is out

title: Die EZB fordert bis Oktober 2026 von Banken konkrete Maßnahmen gegen KI-gestützte Cyberangriffe, die jede Verteidigungsreaktion drastisch beschleunigen müssen. Informatiker sollten jetzt Segmentierung, kontinuierliche Attack-Surface-Discovery und vollständige Asset-Inventare ins Engineering-Backlog priorisieren.  #Aktuell #Strategie #Cloud #DataBreach #EZB #I... https://www.it-finanzmagazin.de/vom-ezb-brief-zum-engineering-backlog-was-bis-zum-31-oktober-auf-den-plan-gehoert-252127/?fsp_sid=46550
text:
Alexander Goller, Illumio Illumio

Audio-Playerhttps://www.it-finanzmagazin.de/wp-content/uploads/speaker/post-252127.mp3?cb=1792588914.mp300:0000:005:44Pfeiltasten Hoch/Runter benutzen, um die Lautstärke zu regeln.

Die EZB-Bankenaufsicht verlangt von allen bedeutenden Instituten bis zum 31. Oktober 2026 einen Maßnahmenplan gegen KI-gestützte Cyberangriffe. Eine technische Übersetzung – jenseits der Compliance-Prosa.
von Alexander Goller, Principal Solutions Architect EMEA bei Illumio
Der Brief der EZB vom 7. Juli 2026 (SSM-2026-0301) lässt sich auf eine Gleichung reduzieren: KI-Modelle verkürzen die Zeit zwischen Schwachstellen-Entdeckung und funktionierendem Exploit – also muss auf der Verteidigerseite jede Kennzahl schrumpfen, die ein Zeitfenster beschreibt: Time-to-Detect, Time-to-Patch, Time-to-Contain, Time-to-Recover.
Nach DORA und dem Cyber-Stresstest 2024 behandelt die Aufsicht KI-gestützte Angriffe als reale, praktische Bedrohung, sie nimmt die Angriffe sehr ernst und verweist ergänzend auf CERT-EU: KI verändert die Ökonomie der Schwachstellensuche. Daraus ergeben sich sechs Handlungsfelder, die darauf zielen, den Vorteil der Angreifer zu verringern, und in denen Segmentierung gleich zweimal auftaucht.
1. Exposure identifizieren
Gefordert: ein Inventar aller ICT-Assets inklusive Drittsoftware und Open Source, dazu kontinuierliche Überwachung aller extern erreichbaren Systeme, Cloud-Umgebungen und VPN-Verbindungen zu Dritten. Das Ziel ist klar: die eigene Exposition erkennen, bevor Angreifer es tun. Technisch heißt das kontinuierliche Attack-Surface-Discovery statt Quartalsscans, ein Asset-Repository mit Ownership, Erreichbarkeit und Kritikalität – und SBOMs für eigene wie zugekaufte Software. Priorität eins laut EZB: Perimeter-Technologien – Gateways, Firewalls, exponierte Appliances.
2. Patchen im Maschinentempo
Ist die Exposition bekannt, geht es im nächsten Schritt darum, das Zeitfenster für Patches zu verkürzen, um damit mögliche Exploits auszuschließen. Priorisiert wird nach realer Ausnutzbarkeit – einschließlich Exploit-Wahrscheinlichkeit (EPSS), bekanntermaßen ausgenutzte Schwachstellen (KEV) – und nicht allein nach dem CVSS-Basiswert.
Den entscheidenden Kontext liefern Vulnerability Maps: Sie verbinden Scanner-Daten mit den realen Kommunikations­be­zie­hungen der Workloads und zeigen, welche Schwachstellen im Netz tatsächlich erreichbar sind.“
Autor Alexander Goller, IllumioAlexander Goller ist Prin­ci­pal So­lu­ti­ons Ar­chi­tect EMEA bei Il­lu­mio (Web­site) un­ter­stützt Un­ter­neh­men da­bei, resi­li­en­ter ge­gen Cy­ber­at­ta­cken zu wer­den und ih­re Mul­ti-Cloud-In­fra­struk­tu­ren durch Vi­si­bi­li­tät und Seg­men­tie­rung ab­zu­si­chern. Er ver­fügt über lang­jäh­ri­ge Er­fah­rung im IT-Si­cher­heits­um­feld und hat als Soft­ware­in­ge­nieur Netz­werk- und Si­cher­heits­soft­ware ent­wi­ckelt. Er kennt die Si­cher­heits­her­aus­for­de­run­gen von Un­ter­neh­men al­ler Bran­chen und Grö­ßen und sieht Au­to­ma­ti­sie­rung, In­fra­struc­tu­re as Code und Cloud-na­ti­ve An­wen­dun­gen als nächs­te Evo­lu­ti­ons­stu­fe der IT-Sicherheit.Erreichbarkeit wird messbar. Dazu eine Emergency-Lane im Change-Management sowie SLAs für beschleunigte Remediation bei Dienstleistern. Wo kein Patch möglich ist, wird Segmentierung zur kompensierenden Kontrolle.
3. Detektion, die mithält
Da Cyberangriffe immer schneller ablaufen, darf sich Detektion nicht mehr nur darum drehen, einen Breach zu erkennen. Der Breach muss auch früh genug erkannt werden, so dass Maßnahmen ergriffen werden können, die den Angriff eindämmen. Erster Schritt: ein ehrliches Coverage-Assessment: Welche Systeme liefern Telemetrie, in welcher Qualität und Latenz? Darauf aufbauend: verhaltensbasierte Erkennung, Anomalie-Erkennung auf Identitäts- und API-Ebene – und Sichtbarkeit in den Ost-West-Verkehr, wo laterale Bewegung stattfindet, lange bevor sie am Perimeter auffällt.

text:
Unverified dark web claim. This report is based on a post observed on a dark web forum. Yazoul Security has not independently verified the authenticity of this claim.
Leak Site Screenshot Screenshot captured at time of discovery. Image blurred to protect victim PII. × Claim Summary
The Qilin ransomware group has allegedly listed GardaWorld, a Canadian security services and risk management firm operating at www.garda.com, on its dark web leak site. According to the threat actor, the attack date is recorded as October 19, 2026. The group has not disclosed the volume of data it purportedly holds, and no data samples have been referenced in the listing metadata reviewed by Yazoul Security.
This claim remains unverified. GardaWorld has not publicly confirmed any incident, and no independent technical evidence has surfaced to corroborate the group’s assertion. The listing should be treated as an unconfirmed allegation at this time.
Threat Actor Profile
qilin is a ransomware operation that has been tracked under various names across the threat intelligence community. Public research specifically cataloguing this group’s tooling and victim count is limited, and our own records do not contain a confirmed total victim count or a verified toolset for this actor. Analysts should therefore treat any capability assessment as provisional.
Based on general patterns observed across comparable ransomware-as-a-service operations, groups operating under this banner have been associated with double extortion tactics - data theft followed by encryption and leak site pressure. However, we cannot confirm specific tools, malware families, or initial access vectors for this group from available data. No public YARA rules or detection signatures tied to this actor were identified in our review. Organizations should rely on behavioral detections for mass file encryption, unusual data staging, and anomalous outbound transfers rather than actor-specific signatures.
Alleged Data Exposure
The leak site entry reportedly names GardaWorld and its domain but provides no stated data volume. The “Claimed Data” field is empty in the listing data reviewed. This is notable: many ransomware groups publish sample files or data trees to lend credibility to their claims. The absence of such material here means there is currently no way to assess what, if anything, was allegedly exfiltrated.
GardaWorld is a large multinational providing physical security, cash handling, and risk consulting services. If the claim were accurate, the potential sensitivity of any exposed data could be significant given the nature of the firm’s client base. That said, this is speculation only - no evidence of exposed data has been produced.
Potential Impact
If the claim is substantiated, potential consequences could include operational disruption, reputational harm, and regulatory scrutiny under Canadian and international data protection regimes. Clients in government, defense, and critical infrastructure sectors may face downstream risk assessments. However, ransomware groups routinely exaggerate or fabricate claims to pressure victims into payment. The lack of disclosed data volume or samples weakens the credibility of this particular listing.
What to Watch For

Official statements from GardaWorld confirming or denying an incident.
Any regulatory filings or breach notifications in Canada.
Publication of data samples by the group, which would raise confidence in the claim.
Follow-on activity such as extortion deadlines or countdown timers on the leak site.
Related advisories in our /advisory/ feed.

Disclaimer
This report is based solely on an unverified claim posted to a ransomware group’s leak site. Nothing herein is confirmed. title: The whole industry just stopped breathing on Wednesday afternoon. October 21st, midday. That's when we realized two serious remote code execution bugs in PHP had snuck up on everyone.https://theperimetersite.com/report/383#vulnerability #databreach #infosec
text:
Threat Wrap
The Code is Public. The Patches Are Missing.

TP

The Perimeter Desk
Threat Wrap

2026-10-21

# The Code is Public. The Patches Are Missing.

The whole industry just stopped breathing on Wednesday afternoon. October 21st, midday. That's when we realized two serious remote code execution bugs in PHP had snuck up on everyone. They showed up with a bit of malice attached. The exploits leaked online before the official patches were ready.

Think about what that means. We are talking about CVE-2026-109618, which carries a CVSS score of 9.2. That isn't just some small hiccup in your code. It is a crack in the floorboards of the web itself. A lot of us track disclosure rules for a living, and this looks like an administrative nightmare. Usually, there's a rhythm to it. Someone finds the flaw. They release the patch. You get a grace period to fix it. Then comes the fine if you didn't.

Here, the sequence has been inverted. The attackers have the map, but the defenders don't even have the lock yet.

The objection here is usually that "most modern environments use containers or WAFs to mitigate RCE." That might be true for a handful of well-funded firms in London or Oslo, but it ignores the millions of legacy servers running outdated versions of PHP in the basement of every mid-sized municipality and local business. The second-order effect isn't just a few breached servers; it is the sudden, desperate scramble of every managed service provider on earth trying to implement "virtual patching" while praying their clients don't notice the gap.

While the technical crowd panics over PHP, the administrative crowd in California is dealing with the fallout of a classic contractor failure. The state has had to warn millions of public school students that their data was stolen during a breach at Educational Testing Service (ETS).

This is where the paperwork becomes fascinatingly messy. ETS is the contractor; the California Department of Education is the client. In these arrangements, there is always a clause about who is responsible for notification and when. The press releases claim "commitment to student privacy," but the reality is likely a series of tense meetings between state lawyers and vendor consultants arguing over whose budget pays for the credit monitoring services.

Education has become an oddly attractive target lately. It ranks fifth among sectors this week with 75 stories, and we've seen 26 new incidents hit the wire today alone. The sector is a goldmine of personally identifiable information held by third parties who are often paid far too little to maintain rigorous security standards.

Then there is the matter of the bill. Chrome Holding Company—the successor to 23andMe—has agreed to pay $6 million to settle with California over a 2023 data breach.

Six million dollars looks like a penalty to some people. To anyone who knows what genetic data sells for on the grey market or what remediation costs, it's a rounding error. It is a licensing fee for negligence. They're settling now so they can skip the discovery process of a trial. That would likely show how systemic the failures were.

The energy sector has the same problem. CenterPoint Energy confirmed a breach affecting over 1.6 million people. The numbers are there, but regulators move like glaciers. A whole generation of students could graduate from those ETS schools in the time it takes for a regulator to issue a real fine.

How does this compare to GDPR? Brussels is more aggressive because they use percentages of global turnover. That actually hurts. A flat six million dollar settlement is just a fixed cost, while a percentage of revenue is a variable risk. Companies will keep pricing breaches into their operational costs until US regulators stop using flat fees.

Other things are happening. CISA and the FBI say the SafePay ransomware gang has hit more than 600 critical infrastructure organizations since 2024. There's also a public proof-of-concept for an […]

Incident

published yesterday

Paradigm Healthcare Services Breach Impacts 970,000 Medi-Cal Members

Paradigm Healthcare Services, a San Francisco-based billing processor for Medi-Cal, reports a data breach affecting over 970,000 individuals. The breach occurred in October 2025 but the full extent of the data exposure was not confirmed until August 2026. Attackers gained access to the company's local network between October 8 and October 15, 2025. Paradigm detected the unauthorized activity on October 13, 2025. The investigation confirmed that the attackers accessed files containing protected health information. The company claims that its primary billing platform, the Student Health Network (SHN), remained isolated and unaffected.The exposed data includes:Full namesDates of birthGenderMedi-Cal member identification numbersThe breach impacted 970,000 members. It also set up a dedicated call center to answer questions from affected members. Notification letters were sent to the impacted individuals on September 14, 2026. It's not clear if the company will be offering complimentary credit monitoring and identity protection.

title: A test account, twelve years old, protected by Password1. Somebody finally sat the exam. The ICO issued a reprimand, but no fine.#CyberSecurity #Ransomware #Passwords #DataBreach #InfoSecSource: https://www.infosecurity-magazine.com/news/children-data-stolen-password1/
text:
Written by

James CokerDeputy Editor, Infosecurity MagazineFollow @ReporterCoker

The personal details of thousands of children and their families were breached in Wales after ransomware attackers compromised an account protected by a ‘Password1’ password, an investigation by the UK’s Information Commissioner’s Office (ICO) has revealed.

The data protection regulator issued a reprimand to Ogi Networks Limited (ONL) and the Local Government Data Unit – Wales, known as Data Cymru, for security failings relating to the November 2024 incident.

Data Cymru is funded by the Welsh government and is tasked with enabling local councils and other organizations to find, collect, analyze and present data effectively.

ONL has acted as Data Cymru's third-party IT service provider since 2012.

How the Attack Unfolded

Attackers gained initial access to Data Cymru’s network via a compromised test account known as ‘Test 2’, which had existed for more than 12 years. It was solely protected by the password ‘Password1’.

Access to this account enabled the threat actor to infiltrate Data Cymru’s network and encrypt 182.7GB of data held on a file servers and an internal database (SQL) server.

Before deploying the ransomware, the attackers exfiltrated 42GB of data from a primary domain controller, a file server and an SQL server. This compromised information related to two projects supporting children and families in Wales, which included the personal data of 3300 people, the majority of whom were children.

David Doodson, head of investigations at the ICO, criticized both organizations, stating: “Password1 is not an appropriate password, it is a wide-open door to nefarious actors. This incident shows how a single weak password, attached to an account that was no longer needed, can leave the door open to a serious cyber-attack that can affect thousands.”

No Fine Issued Over Incident

Both ONL and Data Cymru were found to have infringed the UK GDPR legislation in various ways.

ONL’s failings included:

Not applying appropriate password-strength and complexity requirements to an account

Not conducting regular audits of accounts it had created within Data Cymru’s network, allowing the operationally unnecessary test account to remain in existence for more than 12 years

Not reviewing local administrator accounts after their initial deployment

Data Cymru was criticized for failings such as not having a contract in place with ONL containing the legally mandated data protection terms required when appointing a sub-processor and for conducting account reviews that were not scheduled or routine and did not cover the full contents of Active Directory.

In its reprimand, published on October 20, the ICO said the infringements by both organizations continued without being identified or addressed.

However, neither organization has received a financial penalty for the infringements. The ICO highlighted remedial action taken following the incident, which included ONL strengthening its account access controls and Data Cymru and ONL entering into a legally compliant data processing contract.

Doodson said, “The lesson for every organization is straightforward: use strong passwords, protect remote access with multi-factor authentication, regularly review every user account, and be completely clear about who is responsible for cyber security when services are outsourced. Basic cybersecurity controls are not optional, and the negative consequences of not having them can be severe.”

The breach compromised shared clusters, AWS keys, and GCP dedicated servers, leading to the exposure of production databases and customer disk copies.**** #cybersecurity #infosec #incident #databreach https://beyondmachines.net/event_details/zeabur-to-shut-down-following-massive-infrastructure-compromise-and-data-theft-y-0-3-m-6/gD2P6Ple2L
text:
Incident

published yesterday

Zeabur to Shut Down Following Massive Infrastructure Compromise and Data Theft

Zeabur, a developer hosting platform, will shut down permanently after a second security breach in two months. The incident occurred between October 14 and October 15, 2026. An external attacker used leaked internal credentials to compromise shared clusters and dedicated servers. This breach follows an earlier August 2026 incident where attackers exploited a Server-Side Request Forgery (SSRF) vulnerability in a customer's NextChat application, tracked as CVE-2023-49785 (CVSS score 7.5), to move into internal systems.The attacker used two paths to enter the network. They first used unexpired cluster admin tokens and AWS keys stored in plaintext in a private configuration repository. These credentials let the attacker access shared clusters in nine regions and the secrets management service. The attacker also used an old Google Cloud Platform (GCP) key to read root passwords stored in plaintext in server settings. They then added a node to the internal network to read the production database.The exposed data includes:3,218,965 environment variable records (names and values)321,810 user accounts with emails, usernames, and phone numbers566 zSend API keys in plaintext11,536 platform access token hashesData from 865 database services including n8n and PostgreSQLDisk copies and data from 101 GCP dedicated serversZeabur revoked all compromised cluster tokens, AWS keys, and GCP service account keys. The team blocked public SSH access to admin interfaces and forced a logout for all users. They reset root passwords for affected GCP servers and removed unauthorized network nodes. The company will end all operations by December 31, 2026. The team decided to stop because the infrastructure is too complex to maintain securely.Users must rotate all secrets, API keys, and database passwords used on the platform. Affected individuals should check GitHub audit logs for unauthorized actions by the Zeabur GitHub App. The company recommends rebuilding all dedicated servers to remove any backdoors.

text:
TeamUpdraft develops UpdraftPlus, a popular backup tool for WordPress websites with over four million active installations, and also operates remote monitoring services.
What evidence fell into the wrong hands?
The exposed customer database included names, email addresses, billing addresses, order history, passwords in encrypted form, two-step authentication settings, and login keys.
The company clarified that customer financial information is not stored on its systems, as it is managed directly by Stripe and PayPal. The UpdraftPlus plugin itself, locally managed versions, and backups sent to user storage were also not affected.

READ ALSO
Meta fined $25 billion for Cambridge Analytica scandal

The action of the attacks
Security researchers observed that the perpetrators used valid connection keys to send commands and secretly install add-ons on October 18 and 19, 2026. Experts identified the dangerous program as acting as a backdoor that intercepts website requests and creates unauthorized accounts.
What did the company do?
TeamUpdraft released versions 1.26.13 for the free version and 2.26.13 for Premium, which automatically disconnect all connections made before 10pm on October 18, 2026. In addition, the company reported the incident to the UK's data protection authority.

title: Midnight Mimosa infecte Android avant le premier démarrage
text:
Des smartphones Android arrivent chez leurs propriétaires avec un logiciel malveillant déjà intégré, capable d’installer des applications discrètement et de détourner leur connexion Internet à des fins frauduleuses.
Midnight Mimosa transforme des téléphones Android à bas prix en supports de fraude publicitaire et, potentiellement, en relais réseau contrôlés à distance. Cette campagne touche des milliers d’appareils dans plus de 150 pays, dont la France. Sa particularité tient à son implantation dans le micrologiciel, le logiciel qui accompagne le matériel et participe au fonctionnement du téléphone. Le propriétaire peut donc recevoir un appareil déjà compromis, sans avoir téléchargé la moindre application suspecte. Les chercheurs décrivent une infection persistante, dotée de privilèges système, dont l’origine exacte dans la chaîne d’approvisionnement reste à établir.
Une infection installée au cœur du téléphone
Le premier téléchargement dangereux n’existe parfois pas. Dans cette affaire, le composant malveillant précède l’utilisateur et bénéficie de droits habituellement réservés au fonctionnement d’Android. Une apparence de service technique suffit ensuite à brouiller les pistes.
Selon les éléments rapportés, le logiciel d’espionnage de téléphone Midnight Mimosa serait actif depuis au moins deux ans. Le Mexique, la France, l’Italie, les États-Unis, l’Allemagne, le Brésil et l’Espagne figurent parmi les pays les plus représentés dans les observations des chercheurs. Ces données décrivent les appareils détectés, sans constituer un recensement exhaustif des victimes.
L’infection concerne notamment des smartphones économiques équipés de plateformes MediaTek, parmi lesquels les Doogee S200 X et Cubot KINGKONG X. Des contrefaçons reproduisant l’apparence de modèles Samsung ou Apple apparaissent également dans les éléments présentés. Cette présence ne permet pas d’attribuer une responsabilité au fournisseur des puces ni aux marques imitées.
Le point d’entrée précis demeure inconnu
L’hypothèse privilégiée est celle d’une introduction au cours de la chaîne d’approvisionnement. Les informations disponibles ne permettent toutefois d’identifier ni l’étape concernée ni les responsables. La découverte d’un composant dans un micrologiciel ne démontre pas, à elle seule, la participation consciente du fabricant.
Le logiciel se présente notamment sous les noms com.android.system.lite et com.android.sys.prot. Ces intitulés évoquent des fonctions internes ordinaires. Derrière cette façade, les composants disposent de signatures et de permissions leur permettant d’agir avec des privilèges élevés. Le gestionnaire d’applications classique ne suffit donc pas à les supprimer. Sur les forums XDA, des propriétaires de téléphones Cubot et Doogee ont signalé le retour d’applications suspectes après leur suppression. Un utilisateur de Doogee Fire 3 Max rapporte une apparition après une mise à jour officielle, suivie d’une disparition après restauration d’un micrologiciel antérieur. Ce témoignage apporte un indice sur son appareil, sans établir un scénario identique pour toute la campagne.
Les capacités décrites dépassent largement l’affichage publicitaire. Midnight Mimosa peut ajouter ou retirer des applications sans solliciter le propriétaire, accorder des autorisations et exécuter du code transmis par ses opérateurs. Le téléphone conserve ainsi un composant capable de renouveler les charges malveillantes.
Publicités invisibles et connexions détournables
Les chercheurs ont recensé environ 32 applications distribuées par ce dispositif. Météo, gestion de fichiers, reconnaissance de texte ou édition audio leur servent de couverture. Ces fonctions familières rendent leur présence moins immédiatement suspecte.
La rémunération repose principalement sur une fraude publicitaire. Les applications utilisent un kit publicitaire légitime pour récupérer de véritables annonces. Leur affichage s’effectue cependant dans des fenêtres invisibles superposées à d’autres […]

title: Des jeux Nintendo Switch tournent sur Xbox Series X
text:
Une démonstration montre plusieurs jeux Nintendo sur Xbox Series X grâce à un émulateur. Cette expérience repose sur le mode développeur, sans jailbreak annoncé de la console.
Faire apparaître Mario sur une Xbox attire immédiatement les regards. Derrière cette démonstration, l’enjeu technique concerne surtout la manière d’exécuter un logiciel conçu pour un autre environnement sans compromettre le système qui l’accueille. Des séquences relayées en ligne montrent plusieurs titres Nintendo fonctionner sur Xbox Series X avec une fluidité visuellement convaincante. Le projet serait dérivé d’Eden, un émulateur Switch adapté à la console Microsoft. Son fonctionnement reposerait sur le mode développeur, dans un espace isolé. L’identité exacte du portage utilisé, ses performances mesurées et sa compatibilité complète restent toutefois insuffisamment documentées dans les éléments fournis.
Une démonstration prometteuse, une portée à préciser
La scène a de quoi surprendre : une console Microsoft affiche des jeux associés à l’univers Nintendo. L’auteur de la démonstration, présenté dans le texte transmis sous le pseudonyme FoxHitoriki, aurait notamment lancé Super Mario Odyssey, Super Mario Wonder et Metroid Prime Beyond. Les images décrites donnent une impression de fluidité, sans fournir les mesures nécessaires pour établir un bilan technique complet.
Cette distinction compte. Une séquence de jeu permet d’observer un fonctionnement à un instant donné. Elle ne suffit pas à démontrer que chaque titre peut être parcouru intégralement, avec un comportement constant et sans anomalie. Aucun relevé de performances, protocole de test ou inventaire détaillé des limitations n’accompagne le récit fourni. La démonstration constitue donc un indice de progression technique, dont la portée doit rester précisément délimitée.
Le projet est présenté comme une adaptation d’Eden, sous le nom NXbox. Cette attribution demeure à formuler au conditionnel : les éléments disponibles ne permettent pas d’identifier avec certitude la version employée dans la vidéo. La documentation publique distingue plusieurs portages, ce qui appelle à la prudence avant d’associer automatiquement les images à un dépôt précis.
Le principe décrit consiste à adapter les demandes graphiques provenant de l’environnement Switch aux capacités de rendu de la Xbox. L’objectif est de permettre à des programmes initialement destinés à une autre machine de fonctionner sur le matériel Microsoft. Il s’agit d’un travail de compatibilité logicielle, dont le résultat visible peut masquer une importante complexité technique.
L’auteur n’aurait communiqué ni explication détaillée ni lien de téléchargement avec sa démonstration. Cette absence limite la possibilité de reproduire exactement l’expérience à partir des seules informations transmises. Elle empêche également d’établir les conditions précises dans lesquelles les jeux ont été exécutés.
Pour le lecteur, la conclusion reste circonscrite : des images présentent plusieurs titres en fonctionnement, tandis que les performances générales et les conditions de reproduction restent à documenter.
Le mode développeur change la lecture cyber
L’élément déterminant concerne le cadre d’exécution. Selon le récit fourni, l’émulateur utilise le mode développeur de la Xbox Series X. Ce fonctionnement crée un environnement isolé destiné à accueillir des applications, sans que la démonstration soit présentée comme un jailbreak de la console.
Cette différence évite une confusion fréquente entre deux situations techniques. Exécuter un logiciel dans un espace prévu pour le développement ne démontre pas, à lui seul, une rupture des protections du système. Rien dans les informations transmises n’établit une exploitation de vulnérabilité, une prise de contrôle générale de la Xbox ou un accès à ses composants protégés.
L’intérêt cyber du sujet réside précisément dans cette frontière. Une console peut accueillir un usage inattendu à travers une fonctionnalité de […]

title: Une puce mémorise les mouvements de l’eau
text:
Une étude portant sur 1 222 participants montre qu’après une assistance par ChatGPT, certains réussissent moins bien et renoncent davantage lorsque l’outil devient indisponible, interrogeant notre autonomie intellectuelle.
L’intelligence artificielle facilite la résolution d’un exercice sans garantir que son utilisateur saura ensuite le réaliser seul. Des expériences rapportées par l’Université de Californie à Berkeley mettent en évidence ce décalage. Des participants disposant de ChatGPT réussissaient initialement mieux certaines tâches. Après le retrait de l’assistant, leur précision diminuait et les abandons augmentaient. Les exercices concernaient les fractions et la compréhension écrite. Ces observations interrogent la place des réponses automatiques dans l’apprentissage, ainsi que la préservation de l’effort personnel. Elles invitent toutefois à distinguer une baisse immédiate de performance d’une dégradation durable des capacités de réflexion.
Réussir avec une IA ne garantit pas de réussir seul
Le moment décisif survient lorsque l’assistance disparaît. Jusqu’alors, les participants peuvent demander un indice, vérifier leur démarche ou obtenir directement une solution. L’exercice avance, la réponse arrive et le résultat semble confirmer l’efficacité du dispositif. Une fois ChatGPT retiré, chacun doit reprendre le raisonnement à son compte.
Les expériences présentées réunissent 1 222 personnes. Dans un test consacré aux fractions, un groupe travaille sans assistance, tandis qu’un autre bénéficie de l’outil conversationnel. Les utilisateurs accompagnés obtiennent d’abord de meilleurs résultats. Après le douzième problème, l’accès à ChatGPT est interrompu. Leur réussite recule alors rapidement, et ils renoncent plus souvent aux questions suivantes. Le compte rendu institutionnel confirme cette évolution de la précision et de la persévérance.
Cette succession est essentielle pour comprendre le résultat. Le bénéfice initial concerne une performance obtenue avec une aide disponible. La phase suivante mesure la capacité à poursuivre une activité après son retrait. Confondre ces deux situations reviendrait à attribuer automatiquement à l’utilisateur une maîtrise qui dépendait peut-être, en partie, de l’assistant.
Une autre expérience, consacrée à la compréhension écrite, fait apparaître une tendance comparable. Le phénomène rapporté dépasse donc le seul calcul de fractions. Il concerne aussi une activité dans laquelle il faut lire, interpréter et choisir une réponse.
Pour autant, le titre affirmant que toute utilisation, même minimale, entrave le développement de la pensée dépasse ce que ces éléments permettent de conclure. Les observations décrivent des comportements dans des tâches précises, après une modification des conditions de travail. Elles ne suffisent pas à établir une diminution générale de l’intelligence, ni une perte irréversible de compétences. La distinction protège la portée du résultat. Une difficulté à continuer seul après une assistance mérite d’être examinée pour elle-même. Il n’est pas nécessaire de la transformer en verdict sur l’ensemble des usages de l’IA pour en comprendre l’enjeu.
Préserver l’effort qui construit la compréhension
Les auteurs mettent en avant la notion de « lutte productive ». L’expression désigne l’effort nécessaire pour progresser face à une difficulté, comprendre un problème et construire ses propres capacités. Chercher, hésiter et reprendre une démarche constituent alors une partie de l’apprentissage.
Une réponse immédiate peut supprimer cette étape. L’utilisateur dispose du résultat attendu sans avoir nécessairement parcouru le chemin qui permettrait de le retrouver. La tâche est terminée, tandis que l’acquisition de la méthode reste incertaine.
L’explication avancée porte également sur le rapport au temps. À force de recevoir une solution en quelques secondes, une recherche personnelle plus longue pourrait devenir difficile à accepter. Les auteurs envisagent ainsi que l’habitude […]

title: Trente Mac mini font revivre le Cray-1
text:
Un musée espagnol a construit une réplique du Cray-1 avec trente anciens Mac mini, une installation qui explique comment plusieurs ordinateurs peuvent unir leurs capacités de calcul.
Le Cray-1 revient sous une forme inattendue. Cinquante ans après son arrivée en 1976, ce supercalculateur emblématique possède une réplique grandeur nature au Musée de l’histoire de l’informatique, en Espagne. Sa structure accueille trente Mac mini, principalement commercialisés en 2012, réunis pour travailler ensemble. Le projet a demandé dix-huit mois de préparation et célèbre également le cinquantième anniversaire d’Apple. Les performances annoncées atteignent jusqu’à 1,5 téraflops sur des calculs matriciels. Cette installation pédagogique permet surtout de comprendre le calcul distribué, tout en rappelant ce que représentait Cray dans l’histoire des machines conçues pour traiter les problèmes scientifiques les plus exigeants.
Cray, un nom majeur du calcul scientifique
Avant de désigner cette étonnante reconstruction, Cray renvoie à un constructeur spécialisé dans les supercalculateurs. Ces ordinateurs sont conçus pour exécuter des calculs particulièrement lourds, avec des applications scientifiques, industrielles et stratégiques. Le nom vient de Seymour Cray, ingénieur américain qui a fondé Cray Research en 1972. Le Cray-1, livré en 1976, est devenu l’une des machines les plus reconnaissables de cette industrie.
Son apparence contribue à sa célébrité. Une structure incurvée, accompagnée d’une banquette, lui donne une silhouette inhabituelle pour un ordinateur. Cette disposition répondait à des contraintes techniques précises. La proximité des composants permettait de raccourcir les liaisons électriques et de limiter les délais de transmission des signaux. Les sièges dissimulaient notamment les alimentations électriques.
Le Cray-1 reposait sur le traitement vectoriel, une architecture adaptée à l’application d’opérations sur des séries de données. Ses usages comprenaient la conception aéronautique, les simulations nucléaires et la cryptographie. Pour les lecteurs intéressés par le renseignement, cette dernière application rappelle le lien ancien entre puissance informatique et traitement de problèmes stratégiques.
La réplique espagnole reprend son enveloppe à l’échelle réelle. À l’intérieur, le travail est confié à des ordinateurs Apple beaucoup plus récents. Il faut donc distinguer la reproduction visuelle du supercalculateur et son architecture informatique. L’installation ne restaure pas les circuits historiques du Cray-1 et ne permet pas, à elle seule, d’affirmer qu’elle reproduit son fonctionnement logiciel. Ce choix sert l’objectif de l’exposition. Les visiteurs peuvent observer comment une tâche de calcul change de dimension lorsqu’elle est répartie entre plusieurs machines. La silhouette historique attire le regard ; les ordinateurs qu’elle abrite rendent visible un principe essentiel du calcul contemporain.
Trente ordinateurs coordonnés dans une même structure
D’après les caractéristiques rapportées dans le texte fourni, l’ensemble comprend cinq Mac mini équipés de processeurs Intel Core i7 à quatre cœurs et vingt-cinq modèles dotés de Core i5 à deux cœurs. L’addition donne soixante-dix cœurs physiques, soit vingt pour les premiers et cinquante pour les seconds. La majorité des appareils datent de 2012. Sur une épreuve de multiplication matricielle, la configuration aurait atteint 1,3 téraflops. Un précédent fonctionnement mobilisant tous les cœurs aurait permis d’obtenir 1,5 téraflops. Ces valeurs décrivent les performances annoncées pour cette charge de travail particulière.
Le Cray-1 d’origine affichait une puissance maximale théorique d’environ 160 mégaflops. La comparaison avec les résultats de la réplique demande donc de la prudence : un plafond théorique et une mesure issue d’un test spécifique ne permettent pas d’établir directement un classement entre les deux architectures. Le musée rapproche deux générations informatiques, […]

State Bank of India Discloses Customer Data Exposure on Dark Web

State Bank of India (SBI) disclosed a potential customer data exposure on October 21, 2026, after being alerted by its threat intelligence provider, the Defence Cyber Agency, and the Indian Computer Emergency Response Team (CERT-In) about data appearing on the dark web. SBI's preliminary analysis of approximately 375,000 records identified 3,897 customer records containing personally identifiable information (PII).The bank is investigating the authenticity, completeness, source, and extent of the exposure and has not confirmed whether the data originated from its own systems or a third party. A threat actor using the name Siriusim also claimed to have released 2,722 PDF documents, including loan applications and account opening forms. SBI has not confirmed those claims.The exposed data includes:Customer namesRegistered mobile numbersDates of birthGenderEmail addressesResidential addressesBranch and Customer Information File (CIF) identifiersLead IDsMetadata associated with loan and lead recordsOther related filesLoan applications and account opening forms (claimed by the threat actor)2,722 PDF documents (claimed by the threat actor)The number of affected individuals has not been disclosed. SBI said the incident has no material impact on its core business operations, financial performance, or business continuity. The bank activated its cyber incident response and containment protocols and engaged an independent cybersecurity agency empanelled by CERT-In to investigate the source and extent of the exposure.SBI customers should monitor their accounts for unfamiliar activity and remain alert for phishing calls, emails, or messages that use personal information to appear legitimate. Customers should avoid sharing passwords, PINs, OTPs, or other banking credentials and verify suspicious communications through official SBI channels.

title: Gaza : dialogue entre un humanitaire et une rabbine. Avec Jean-François Corty & Nava Hefetz
text:
Gaza : dialogue entre un humanitaire et une rabbine. Avec Jean-François Corty & Nava Hefetz

1 min. de lecture

Citer

Partager

Imprimeren PDF

Ajouter aux favoris

Pascal Boniface

Directeur de l’IRIS

Jean-François Corty

Chercheur associé à l’IRIS, président de Médecins du monde

Nava Hefetz
Rabbine et activiste israélienne

La riposte israélienne aux attentats du 7 octobre 2023 a lourdement frappé la population civile de Gaza et de nombreuses instances internationales et ONG qualifient les actes commis par les forces israéliennes de génocide. Les enfants se retrouvent particulièrement exposés. Parmi les survivants, nombreux sont les orphelins laissés sans perspectives. En parallèle, la Cisjordanie souffre depuis plusieurs décennies de l’expansion de l’occupation israélienne, qui expose elle aussi les Palestiniens à la privation et la répression, parfois mortelle.Ce désastre humanitaire a amené Jean-François Corty, médecin humanitaire français, et Nava Hefetz, rabbine israélienne, à agir de concert dans le cadre d’un projet d’évacuation d’enfants gazaouis vers la France. Malgré l’échec de cette entreprise, et leurs visions et opinions divergentes sur certains aspects du conflit, ils poursuivent un dialogue respectueux et un combat commun pour défendre les droits humains fondamentaux à Gaza et en Cisjordanie.

Comment dépasser les divergences d’opinion afin de poursuivre un objectif commun ? Les Accords d’Abraham (2020) ont-ils contribué à normaliser la colonisation ? Le boycott des biens en provenance d’Israël et de ses colonies pourrait-il constituer un levier efficace pour lutter contre la colonisation ? Peut-on qualifier les crimes commis par l’État israélien de génocide ?

Autant d’enjeux abordés avec Jean-François Corty, président de Médecins du monde et chercheur associé à l’IRIS, et Nava Hefetz, rabbine et activiste israélienne.

The Russia-linked state-sponsored threat actor tracked as APT28 (aka BlueDelta, Fancy Bear, and Forest Blizzard) has been attributed to attacks targeting two member states of the North Atlantic Treaty Organization (NATO).

The Symantec Threat Hunter Team, which is tracking the activity cluster under the moniker Swallowtail, involved the use of a backdoor called HOOKEDGE and a previously undocumented loader that is designed to decrypt and run an encrypted payload in memory by using a cryptographic key that's supplied at runtime.

Targets of the activity included a law enforcement agency, a naval shipbuilder, and a manufacturer of military aircraft engines – entities that hold information that could be of use to a foreign intelligence agency, the Broadcom-owned threat intelligence unit said.

"During one attack against the naval shipbuilder, operators returned to a compromised host repeatedly over the course of a week in what appeared to be hands-on-keyboard activity," Symantec said in a report shared with The Hacker News. "They stole credential material using two separate techniques, opened a persistent SSH tunnel into the organization's internal network and deployed a previously undocumented reflective loader."

APT28's use of HOOKEDGE was first publicly documented by Recorded Future Insikt Group in late August 2026 in connection with a cyber espionage campaign targeting government and diplomatic organizations in Romania, Spain, and Türkiye between September 2025 and early April 2026.

HOOKEDGE shares significant code and tradecraft overlap with HEADLACE, a modular Windows implant that APT28 has put to use in attacks targeting diplomats since April 2023. Delivered via spear-phishing lures, HOOKEDGE is a barebones Windows batch script that's capable of accepting attacker-issued commands and sending the results back.

The backdoor is delivered via macro-enabled Microsoft Word documents and communicates entirely through a webhook[.]site URL, which acts as a channel to stage tasks and to receive execution output. Infected machines then fetch these tasks using a hidden, off-screen instance of the Microsoft Edge browser as opposed to relying on a traditional downloader.

In the attack aimed at the naval shipbuilder in late July 2026, the threat actors are said to have delivered new variants of HOOKEDGE that abandon the use of webhook[.]site in favor of a dedicated IP address ("185.82.218[.]119:443") for both tasking and exfiltration.

"The attackers used two distinct credential-theft techniques," Symantec said. "In one, they pushed an SSH private key onto the compromised host and immediately used it to open an SSH connection back to their own server, requesting a persistent, backgrounded tunnel that would give them a route from their infrastructure into the target's internal network."

"In the other, they ran a short, self-contained PowerShell script that stands up a listener on the host's own loopback address and forces the machine to authenticate to it, capturing the resulting NTLM handshake."

The attackers have also been observed dropping a new reflective loader ("ld.exe") using a curl command via SSH that's engineered to decode and run a next-stage component. The exact nature of the payload remains unknown.
The most recent activity was registered on September 24, 2026, when a Visual Basic Script launcher associated with HOOKEDGE was observed within the shipbuilder's network. It's unclear if any data was stolen as a result of these intrusions.

As Android Central reports, users have received unexpected emails telling them their phone number has been verified for secondary Google accounts.Like me and many others, you may have one Google account for everyday use, another for work, and a third for things you would rather keep separate. But if you’re using an Android phone, those accounts may have something in common that you didn’t intend or even know about: your phone number.Google’s own documentation confirms that phone number verification is on by default and adds your number to all Google accounts signed in on the device. This applies to both existing accounts and any you add later.Google says phone number verification helps support features such as signing in, account recovery, Rich Communications Services (RCS) messaging, and finding or securing a lost device.But it also means that a number you intended to use with your main account can become associated with a secondary account simply because both are signed in on the same Android device.If you deliberately left your phone number off a secondary account, this links it to your real identity without you knowingly making that connection. Muse, the new general-purpose AI agent from Meta, can expose sensitive information when users share conversations through web links, researchers reported Monday. In response to questions from Ars about the behavior, Meta said it’s suspending the sharing feature while the company reviews it and considers making changes.
Like many online services, Muse has allowed users to share searches, conversations, images, and similar content with other people. Such share features usually involve clicking an option to create a unique URL that anyone can use to load a page hosting the content. To keep potentially sensitive information from being accessible to unintended people, the URLs typically contain a long sequence of text that can’t be easily guessed.
A single query is all that’s required
Muse, which Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg said last month was “built from the ground up for privacy and security,” seems to take the same precautions. But a central design decision for constructing URLs has made the links easy to discover. As a result, researchers from security firm Claroc said they were able to enumerate 6,800 links Muse users created for sharing conversations with others. After opening a few hundred of them, the researchers found information that was clearly not intended to be publicly available, including:

a candidate’s notes preparing for a confidential executive-search call with a frontier AI lab, naming the lab’s internal contact and the meeting time
a national marketing company’s internal revenue review, marked for its CEO
a small-business owner’s loan application, with the amount requested
a to-do list that included a bank fraud alert, with a partial account number and a transaction amount and time
a real-estate investor’s internal performance report, with two property addresses and exact return, income, and mortgage figures
a workplace’s full-year staff vacation calendar, listing dozens of employees against the week each one would be away

“If you had asked us beforehand, we would have guessed that gathering these would take real effort,” the researchers wrote. “It took one query.”
In an emailed statement responding to questions from Ars, Meta said:
We opened the Muse bug bounty program so researchers could raise different scenarios and help us continue improving the product. People have the ability to share specific Muse artifacts, which creates a page that can be accessed by those with the link. However, we’ve paused this functionality while we review this report and consider changes to how these links can be discovered.
Asaf Aprozper, the co-founder and CTO of Claroc, said he reported the findings through Meta’s bug bounty program on October 8 and also tried reaching people at Meta on LinkedIn, but got no reply either way.
The easiest way to discover the URLs is to perform a passive DNS search through one of many available commercial services. Passive DNS records store the historical resolution of domain names to IP addresses, as well as nameserver, and mail-server records over time. Passive DNS systems typically collect DNS responses from sensors positioned at recursive DNS resolvers or other infrastructure. A passive DNS record is generally created when a monitoring system observes a DNS response. In the case here, once the intended party clicks on the share link, the DNS information is recorded in a searchable database.

Claroc researchers were able to discover the Muse share links because all of them use the domain name cf.metaaiusercontent.com. Discovery is further made easy by the decision to add the conversation name to the URL, along with a long string of text. Simplified examples of such links are home-sale-budget-9f21c8a3.cf.metaaiusercontent.com, q3-revenue-review-7b1e42f0.cf.metaaiusercontent.com, and loan-application-draft-a4c9e2.cf.metaaiusercontent.com.
