Effective and efficient use of complex agentic systems is important for all organizations, but recognizing, preventing and recovering from them going rogue could be an existential necessity.

NIST, the NSA, and CISA recognize the increasing potential for AI agents to behave in an unexpected and potentially harmful manner, and has responded with a list of key practices for both preparing for and responding to such behavior. The report (Key Practices for Incident Readiness and Response in Super Intelligence Training and Evaluation) uses the term super intelligence (SI) rather than artificial intelligence (AI) in line with presidential executive order 14434.

In the report, the ten key practices are grouped into five stages: prepare, detect, respond, recover, and report. For clarity, the report also includes three useful terminology definitions covering AI agents, AI control incident, and AI control near-miss.

“The practices are intended to help the frontier SI industry prevent, prepare for, and respond rapidly to incidents in which SI systems do not act as intended or authorized,” the agencies explain.

Preparation includes activities such as asset and risk inventories, defense-in-depth, least privilege, zero-trust controls, credential management, supply chain risk management and more.

Detection requires continuous monitoring for correct behavior, and anomalous activity and indications of compromise.

Response entails isolating affected systems, revoking credentials, rebuilding compromised environments, determining the blast radius, and conducting root-cause analysis that looks past the specific vulnerability exploited.

Recovery requires testing restoration procedures in advance and documenting recovery decisions along with any residual risk accepted.

Reporting requirements are three-fold: report incidents to all affected parties, wherever required by law, and publicly and widely.

None of the stages or practices is given any greater weight over the others. Instead, the five stages should be treated as a single target. Complex agents all have the potential for misbehavior bordering on rogue and dangerous. These ten practices combine to help organizations develop a stable and effective environment for complex agentic systems, where problems can be detected early and effective operation maintained.

Only the final two practices (#9 and #10 in the Report stage) go beyond the more technical steps of incident readiness and response.

The first of these, ‘Notify Government’, may be a legal requirement, including: “Adhere to any applicable legal reporting requirements, including cybersecurity incident reporting obligations to CISA, law enforcement, and/or cyber-defense organizations.”

The last, Share Information Publicly, is mainstream good behavior throughout cybersecurity that will benefit everyone: “Share details with the public, where appropriate, as early as feasible,” and “Identify and publicly report key practices, takeaways, or improvements adopted in response to the incident or that could benefit other actors in the ecosystem.”

The value of this document is not in providing any new or unrecognized information for AI agent governance, but in providing a very clear and thorough checklist for use by security professionals to maximize the use of agents while minimizing or recovering from agentic incidents.

Chrome flags malicious commands that scammers pass off as fixes

Google is updating Chrome’s Enhanced Protection mode to detect scam websites and warn users when a page tricks them into copying a malicious command.
The company introduced Enhanced Protection for Chrome’s Safe Browsing feature in 2020 to address online scams and social engineering. Google says further updates have made its users ten times safer from phishing, social engineering, notification abuse, and other scams compared with those using Standard Protection. The figure is based on a comparison of the average number of safety warnings shown to users of the two modes.
Suspicious sites trigger new alerts
Suspicious site warnings alert users when a page displays deceptive patterns associated with known malicious sites. Their format, icons, colors, and text are tailored to help users decide how to proceed.
“By tailoring the warning UI in this way, we are able to safely expand our coverage to display a higher volume of protective warnings,” Jasika Bawa, Group Product Manager for Chrome, explained.
Dangerous site warnings appear when a page is known to be malicious and poses a high risk of harm. These will continue to use Chrome’s full-page red warning screen.

Dangerous site warnings in Chrome (Source: Google)

Gemini expands scam detection
Google has moved Chrome’s Gemini-powered scam detection from an on-device model to a server-side model for Enhanced Protection users. The feature now checks for fake antivirus and browser update scams in addition to tech support scams.
The model analyzes page content to assess indicators such as the brand being represented, the page’s intent, and the likelihood of a scam. Safe Browsing combines Gemini’s analysis with domain reputation and other security signals to reach a final verdict.
Google says page text is sent for analysis only when a site shows high-confidence scam indicators. The content is processed without being logged, retained, or used to train models.
New warnings target ClickFix scams
ClickFix scams instruct users to “fix” a fake problem by copying and running a malicious command on their computers. The copied command can differ from the one displayed on the page.

A ClickFix scam (Source: Google)

These commands often invoke living-off-the-land binaries (LOLBins), legitimate tools and executables preinstalled on an operating system, such as PowerShell and cmd.exe. Attackers repurpose them to download and install malware, conceal their activity, and take advantage of the trust security software places in them.
Moving the download process from the browser to the terminal allows attackers to bypass Chrome and Safe Browsing download protections.
When Enhanced Protection users copy suspicious commands, Chrome removes personally identifiable information (PII) from the clipboard payload and sends it to Safe Browsing for analysis. A warning appears if the command is deemed dangerous.

Accenture, Dragos and the SANS Institute on Tuesday announced the Community Cyber Resilience Foundation, which aims to help under-resourced US water, electric and natural gas utilities protect their operational technology (OT) environments.

They are putting up roughly $10 million to start, a mix of funding and services. The first phase will cover up to 500 utilities, which will get free security tools, equipment, deployment help and training.

To qualify, a water, wastewater, electric or natural gas utility must be based in the US and bring in under $100 million a year. The companies estimate that this bar covers more than 50,000 organizations, or over 97% of US utilities.

Each participant gets the Dragos Platform and related services, with Accenture handling setup, integration and continued support. SANS will train utility staff in ICS/OT security so they can run their defenses internally.

The foundation will also fund the hardware needed to deploy and run the Dragos Platform. It will connect participants to a peer network of utilities that share operational experience.

The companies say many small utilities struggle with limited funding, workforce shortages and aging technology, especially those serving rural or underserved communities. They also cited recent attacks on more than 100 US water systems across over a dozen states.

“Adversaries are aggressively targeting utilities, attacking the operational environments that provide life-sustaining services to millions of Americans. Yet many small operators lack the capacity to defend against these threats,” said Dragos CEO Robert M. Lee.

The foundation builds on the Dragos Community Defense Program, which gives more than 100 utilities free access to the Dragos Platform. Dragos launched that program in December 2023 for US utilities with less than $100 million in annual revenue.

The announcement comes four months after Accenture agreed to acquire a majority stake in Dragos. The deal was part of an OT cybersecurity push valued at roughly $4.1 billion.
